# Agentic Engineering Workflow — Complete Setup Guide

*A full walkthrough of Kun's agentic engineering workflow, as presented in the video. All tools are free, open-source, and agent-agnostic. This guide gives you everything you need to recreate this workflow in your own terminal.*

---

## Layer 0: The Terminal Stack (The Ship)

The workflow is terminal-centric — everything happens in the keyboard with zero mouse dependency. This enables the same setup on a laptop, desktop, or even phone via SSH.

### Components

| Tool | Purpose | Install Command |
|------|---------|-----------------|
| **WezTerm** | Cross-platform terminal emulator (Windows/Mac/Linux identical). Highly customizable via Lua scripting with hot-reload. | [wezterm.org](https://wezterm.org) or `brew install wezterm` |
| **tmux** | Terminal multiplexer — persistent sessions, multi-pane, multi-tab (windows), detach/re-attach across devices. | `brew install tmux` |
| **NeoVim** | Modern Vim — keyboard-only editor with relative line numbers, fuzzy file finding, codebase search. | `brew install neovim` |

### Why Terminal-Centric

- All apps designed for keyboard — hands never leave home row [1][4]
- tmux sessions persist on a server; detach from one device and re-attach from another with full state [1][2]
- Split into multiple panes (agent / editor / shell) and multiple tabs (parallel agent sessions) [1][2]
- The exact same workflow works on your phone via SSH [1][4]

### tmux Config (Recommended)

Customize tmux with keybinds for:
- Splitting panes
- Creating/switching tabs (windows)
- A status bar showing session info and agent activity

> ⚠️ Default tmux is bare. Invest time in configuration — many YouTube tutorials cover tmux theming and keybind setup [1].

---

## Layer 1: Agent Harnesses (The Crew Mates)

The workflow is **agent-agnostic** — everything applies regardless of which harness or model you use. The speaker uses four regularly:

| Harness | When to Use |
|---------|-------------|
| **Claude Code** | Primary choice — best default experience, rich feature set, practical for Anthropic subscription users [1][4][9] |
| **Cursor** | GUI-based when preferred |
| **Aider** | Lightweight alternative |
| **Open Code** | Solid open-source choice [1][2] |

> The landscape changes fast. The workflow is designed so you can swap harnesses without changing your processes [1][2].

---

## Layer 2: Memory System (Onboarding the Crew)

Fresh agents know nothing about you or your project. You onboard them through **memory files** and **skills**.

### 2a. Global Memory File (`agents.md` / `CLAUDE.md`)

**Location:**
- Claude Code: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
- Other agents: standard location varies

**Key trick:** Symlink them so one file serves all:
```bash
ln -s ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md ~/.claude/agents.md
```

**Content (keep ~27 lines — minimal!):**
- Personal preferences (e.g., "never use mdash, use plain dash instead")
- "When making technical decisions, don't give too much weight to development cost" — AI underestimates its own speed and will bias toward cheap/low-quality solutions if not corrected [1][4]
- "When doing bug fixes, always start with reproducing the bug in an end-to-end setting" — unit tests alone are insufficient [1][4][10]
- [`opinions.md`](https://kunnaphat.dev) — a separate concept for nuanced opinions (linked in the video description)

> Everything in this file goes into every single agent session's system prompt across all projects. Keep it tight to avoid silent token waste [1][3].

### 2b. Project-Level Memory File (`CLAUDE.md` / `agents.md` per repo)

**Content:**
- What the project is
- How the repo is laid out
- Key terminology
- How important components work
- How to do end-to-end testing
- Conventions and learned patterns [2][3][4]

**How to build it:** Don't write it by hand. Every time an agent does something wrong, correct it and say: "Remember this and store it in the memory file." Over time, agents on this project get smarter automatically [2][3].

### 2c. Skills (Progressive Disclosure)

When the memory file gets bloated, **extract conditionally-needed knowledge into skills**. Example: end-to-end testing instructions are only needed when making changes, not when answering questions [1][2].

**How skills work:**
- When an agent starts, it loads only the **short description** field from each skill into the system prompt
- Only when the agent decides it needs a skill does it read the full file
- This lets you store massive knowledge without bloating every request [1][7]

**Installing the Skill Creator (so agents can create skills for you):**
```bash
npx skills --install skill-creator
```
This CLI from Vercel manages skills and works with any agent harness. Once installed, just tell your agent: "Extract the end-to-end testing instructions from our agents.md into a project-level skill" [1][2][5].

**⚠️ Warning on third-party skills:**
- Do not install random skills from the internet, even ones with many GitHub stars [1][7]
- Skills can instruct agents to run arbitrary code and leak credentials [1][7]
- Many popular skills have never been rigorously evaluated and can degrade agent performance (e.g., one 177K-star skill used 5% more tokens with worse results) [1][7]

---

## Layer 3: Voice Input (Faster Communication)

Talking is ~3x faster than typing (Stanford study cited in the transcripts) [1][2]. The workflow uses voice input for all agent interactions.

**Setup:**
- Use **OpenAI Whisper** or **SuperWhisperer** for transcription [1][10]
- Customize the transcription model's system prompt with your project-specific vocabulary for better recognition (e.g., project names like "Lavish", "Hibbit", "AXI") [1][10]

---

## Layer 4: Tool Design — AXI Standards

Agents depend on external tools. The design of these tools dramatically affects performance. The speaker created **AXI** — a set of 10 design principles for making tools efficient for agents [1][8][9].

**Key example (GitHub):**

| Method | Token Cost | Latency | Success Rate |
|--------|-----------|---------|--------------|
| GitHub MCP Server | 3x baseline | 2x+ baseline | Baseline |
| GitHub CLI (native) | Better | Better | Better |
| **GitHub AXI** | **Lowest** | **Lowest** | **Highest** |

Using GitHub MCP wastes both time and money for no benefit [1][8]. AXI tools use token-efficient output formats (saving ~40% over JSON) and treat agents as first-class citizens [8][9].

**AXI catalog:** Available at [axi.md](https://axi.md). Includes:
- **GitHub AXI** — lowest cost, highest success rate for GitHub operations
- **Chrome DevTools AXI** — fewer turns, fewer tokens than other browser automation tools
- **Lavish AXI** — the planning tool (see Layer 5)

---

## Layer 5: The Workflow — Step by Step

### Step 1: Planning with Lavish 🏗️

Instead of letting the agent dump a wall of text in the terminal:

1. Describe the feature you want (using voice input)
2. The agent (with Lavish skill installed) creates an **interactive HTML artifact** in your browser
3. The artifact uses the **same design system as your project** — it looks like your actual app
4. You can **annotate specific parts**, make comments, and click options to make decisions
5. Feedback goes back to the agent **inside Lavish** — no need to go back to the terminal [1][5][9]

> "I can never go back to reading text in the terminal anymore." [1][3]

### Step 2: Hands-Off Implementation 🤖

After planning is complete:
1. Tell the agent: "Start building."
2. **Do not interfere** — the agent works autonomously from the clarified requirements
3. Only come back when the agent says it's done [1][3][6]

### Step 3: No Mistakes Pipeline (Don't Review Diffs!) ✅

When the agent says "done", **do not review the diff.** That creates a bottleneck — you can only review so many diffs per day. Instead, think like an engineering director: create good processes and let the team execute them [1][3][6].

**Trigger the No Mistakes pipeline:**
```bash
# As a command, or just type "no mistakes" to the agent
```

**Pipeline stages (fully automated):**
1. Create a branch (if one doesn't exist) and commit the changes [1][4]
2. Move to an **isolated git worktree** — validation never touches your working repo [1][4]
3. **Analyze the original intent** by reading the agent session [1][4]
4. **Rebase onto latest main** from remote origin and resolve merge conflicts up front [1][4]
5. **Adversarial review** in a fresh context window — most problems caught here; obvious ones self-corrected, ambiguous ones with product implications escalated to you [1][4][7]
6. **End-to-end test** against original intent — records evidence (screenshots, videos, logs) proving the change works [1][4][7]
7. **Documentation pass** — updates all relevant docs [1][4]
8. **Check for linking/lint issues** [1][4]
9. **Push branch and raise a PR** with a summary of intent, changes, testing evidence, and pipeline results [1][2][4]
10. **Babysit the PR** until merged — handles merge conflicts and CI failures automatically [1][4][7]

**Risk assessment in the PR:**
- **Low-risk changes:** Don't review the diff at all — the pipeline has validated thoroughly [1][7][8]
- **High-risk changes:** Spend time reviewing in detail [1][7][8]

### Step 4: Long-Running Loops with "Good Night, Have Fun" 🌙

For tasks that take hours (e.g., overnight usability testing):
```bash
good-night-have-fun --objective "Pretend you are a 7-year-old and use the app end-to-end. Find the first usability problem. Fix it. Repeat until no problems remain."
```

**Features:**
- Precise **token caps**, **iteration caps**, and **stop conditions** [1][5][8]
- Monitors iterations (shown as moon icons) and commits made [1][5]
- Better than built-in `/go` commands because it won't burn your entire weekly quota overnight [1][5]
- Best for **verifiable objectives**: reducing page load time, improving test coverage, metric optimization, automated research [1][3][8]

---

## Layer 6: Parallel Agents (Multiple Crew Mates)

### The Problem

Running multiple agents in the same directory causes conflicts. The native solution is `git worktree`:
```bash
git worktree add ../my-project-feature-branch feature-branch
```
But manual worktree management becomes cognitive debt — you must track which worktrees are active, what they're doing, and clean them up [3][4].

### The Solution: Treehouse 🌳

```bash
# Create a fresh worktree and drop into it
treehouse

# See all worktrees and their status
treehouse status

# Close the tab when done — Treehouse auto-recycles it
```

Treehouse:
- Creates fresh worktrees on demand
- Tracks which are in use vs. idle
- Auto-recycles idle worktrees for future use
- No cognitive overhead of manual management [3][4][5]

### Running Parallel Sessions

1. Spin up a new tmux tab
2. Run `treehouse` to get an isolated worktree
3. Launch your agent in that worktree
4. Give it a task and tell it to run No Mistakes when done
5. Switch between tabs via keyboard shortcuts — monitor status from the tmux bar [3][4]

The speaker regularly runs 3+ agents in parallel, each working on different features [3].

---

## Layer 7: First Mate — The Ultimate Level-Up 🧑‍✈️

Managing many parallel sessions yourself becomes exhausting — constant context switching, tracking what each session is doing [1][3][8].

**First Mate** is a free, open-source meta-agent that acts as your single point of contact:

```bash
git clone <first-mate-repo>
cd first-mate
# Run an agent in this repo and talk to it
```

**What First Mate does:**
1. You speak to First Mate via voice (it uses SuperWhisperer with custom vocabulary for perfect transcription of project names) [1][3][10]
2. You describe high-level goals: "For all three projects, add an update command that updates their version to latest on npm" [1][3]
3. First Mate realizes this is 3 parallel tasks, spins up tmux tabs, uses Treehouse for isolated worktrees, runs agents in each, runs No Mistakes on every change, and gets PRs ready [1][3]
4. Meanwhile, you can give it more work: "Look at the three most recent open issues in the Lavish AXI repo" — it pulls issues while waiting for background agents [1][3]
5. You discuss which issues are actionable, then say "Address issue #87" — First Mate queues it up [1][3]

**Outcome:** The bottleneck shifts from managing agents to **having enough good ideas** for what to build next. This is the sign you've successfully transitioned from sailor to captain [1][5][10].

---

## Summary: Your Time Allocation as Captain

| Phase | What You Do | Tool |
|-------|-------------|------|
| **Beginning** 🎯 | Clarify requirements, explore options, make decisions | Lavish (visual planning) |
| **Middle** 🤖 | Nothing — AI does all implementation | Agent + Treehouse (parallel worktrees) |
| **End** ✅ | Hold quality bar: assess risk, review high-risk diffs, merge | No Mistakes pipeline (PR with evidence) |
| **Overnight** 🌙 | Sleep while agents run | Good Night, Have Fun |
| **Orchestration** 🧑‍✈️ | Give high-level direction to First Mate | First Mate (delegates to all the above) |

> "The more time I can free up in the middle, the more work I can go do in parallel." [1][3][7]

conversations.question: summarise the key insights from this video

answers.title: rag_llm (single-hop)
answers.answer: The hosts Damian and Jeremy present a monthly data summary of Australian property markets using their Suburb Data platform. Key insights include: most markets have picked up over the last year, with Perth and Darwin as high flyers, while Canberra, Melbourne, Sydney lagging [1][3]. The recent month (May) showed a flat market overall, with Sydney and Melbourne declining 2–2.2% in typical value, while Darwin increased 2.4% [6]. Stock on market increased after the federal budget announcement but remains low in some areas (e.g., Darwin at 0.7%) [6][7]. Days on market increased, indicating a slowing market [9]. Vacancy rates remain very tight (e.g., Darwin 0.4%) [9]. Rental growth was 11.7% over the last 12 months, expected to continue [10]. Units are more affordable and holding up better than houses; opportunities exist in Sydney's western corridor (e.g., Punchbowl under $600k) [8][10]. They emphasize considering granular data, market cycle timing, personal budget, and yield [5][10]. The DSR metric and typical value are used for analysis, with Melbourne moving up in DSR due to algorithm adjustments [4]. The hosts note upcoming impacts from CGT and negative gearing changes [1][3].

The video, part of the Suburb Data podcast, presents a monthly analysis of Australian property markets using data from the Suburb Data platform [1]. Over the past year, most markets have risen, with Darwin and Perth as high flyers, while Canberra, Melbourne, and Sydney lagged [3]. For May, the market was flat overall; Sydney and Melbourne saw monthly declines of about 2%, while Darwin rose 2.4% [6]. Stock on market increased across most cities except Hobart and Adelaide [4][7]. Days on market lifted, indicating a slowing market [9]. Vacancy rates remain very tight, especially in Darwin at 0.4% [9]. Rental growth continues due to low vacancies [10]. The hosts note potential impacts from CGT and negative gearing changes [3]. They emphasize considering market cycle timing and budget, and that units may be holding up better than houses, with opportunities in Sydney's unit market [8][10]. The hosts plan to release monthly updates [1][2].

The chunks refer to DSR 3 as a flagship metric used for shortlisting markets and ranking them by investment quality [s1.5]. However, the provided chunks do not define the algorithm, its components, or how the score is calculated. The explanation is limited to these contextual remarks.

The chunks reference federal budget proposed changes, specifically mentioning CGT and negative gearing adjustments [s3.1][s3.4]. The announcement led to an observed increase in stock on market as investors reacted [s3.1]. The hosts discuss cash flow implications and a wait-and-see approach among investors, but do not detail the specific policy measures or their exact provisions [s3.1][s3.4]. The exact announcements are not described in the provided chunks.

I now have enough evidence from across the transcript to give you a comprehensive summary. Here are the key insights from the video.

## Key Findings
1. The Australian property market is sharply divided, with Perth (+25% annually), Darwin, Brisbane, and Adelaide surging while Sydney, Melbourne, and Canberra lag significantly [2][3].
2. Darwin has emerged as a uniquely compelling market with the tightest vacancy rates (0.3%), double-digit rental growth (15% houses, 11.7% units), and unit prices still under $500K [5][8].
3. Proposed federal CGT and negative gearing changes are already impacting market behaviour, with stock on market and days on market rising as investors pause [1][7].
4. The rental crisis is expected to worsen — the hosts believe the tax changes will push more established properties to owner-occupiers, reducing rental supply and driving vacancy rates even lower [4][7].
5. Units are outperforming houses in relative affordability and are being identified as a key opportunity, especially in Sydney where pockets like Punchbowl offer units under $600K [1][9].
6. The hosts advise investors there is no rush to buy and recommend waiting 1–2 months to see how data flows through after the budget announcement [4][9].
7. Markets within markets are critical — even in underperforming cities like Sydney and Melbourne, specific pockets (e.g., Campbelltown, parts of western Sydney) show strong DSR 3 scores [4][8].

## Finding 1: Stark divergence between high-flying and lagging capital cities

Over the last 12 months, Perth has been the standout performer with extraordinary 25% annual growth and roughly 100% growth over 5 years, followed closely by Brisbane (95% over 5 years) and Adelaide (nearly 90% over 5 years) [2][3]. In contrast, Sydney, Melbourne, and Canberra are lagging, with Sydney's typical values actually declining by around 2.2% in a single month and Melbourne slipping by a similar margin [8]. However, the hosts stress that even in weaker cities there are strong pockets — Sydney has roughly 700 suburbs, Melbourne around 500, so generalisations mask significant variation [8][9].

## Finding 2: Darwin — the most compelling opportunity in the country

Darwin presents a unique combination of metrics: it has the tightest vacancy rate in the nation at just 0.3% (down from 0.6%), 15% annual rental growth for houses and 11.7% for units, and yet its unit typical value sits around $430K — a state capital under $500K [5][10]. The hosts push back against the popular media narrative that Darwin is an investor-dominated market, explaining that if it were, vacancy rates would spike when multiple investor properties hit the market simultaneously, whereas Darwin's vacancy rate is actually falling [8]. They acknowledge higher insurance costs in Darwin but describe the yields as "very enticing" for investors with budgets around the $400K range [5].

## Finding 3: Federal budget tax changes driving market uncertainty and slowing activity

The video was recorded shortly after the federal budget announcement of proposed CGT and negative gearing changes (still working through the upper house at the time) [6][7]. While the absolute levels remain tight (a normal market would see ~60 days on market), the trend is clearly one of slowing activity [7]. One host describes a "significantly mixed" picture with polar opposites between markets [10].

## Finding 4: Rental crisis set to deepen, not ease

The hosts are pessimistic about the rental outlook. They argue the federal tax changes will push established property sales toward owner-occupiers rather than investors, which means fewer rentals available in established areas [7]. This dynamic, they say, will push vacancy rates even lower and rents even higher, until cash flow positive property returns to established areas and eventually brings investors back to restore balance [7]. The hosts highlight that units are "holding up a little bit better than houses" simply because of price points — they are far more affordable [1]. For investors, the key question is price point — they advise dialling in on budget and yield, noting that with Melbourne house typical values around $1.2 million, a Perth townhouse or a Darwin unit offers a dramatically cheaper entry point [3][10].

One of the hosts explicitly states, "I don't think there's anything wrong with waiting a couple months just to sort of see what's going on," noting that "everyone's going to tell you there's always an opportunity, but I think you don't need to rush right now" [4]. The hosts emphasise that the next 1–2 months of data will be critical to see how the proposed tax changes truly impact the market [2].

## Finding 7: DSR 3 metric and market cycle timing are critical for smart investing

The hosts use their proprietary DSR 3 (their "flagship metric") to rank and shortlist capital city markets [3]. They note that while Perth and Brisbane top the DSR 3 rankings, their market cycle timing numbers are low because they have already had massive runs (doubling in 5 years) [3]. By contrast, Canberra and Melbourne have high market cycle timing scores precisely because they have been lagging, which could signal opportunity for longer-term investors [4][9]. The key takeaway: market cycle timing is just one input and must be considered alongside all other metrics — and every investment decision ultimately comes down to individual budget, goals, and strategy [10][1].

answers.answer: Herder is a terminal multiplexer that you run inside a terminal emulator (e.g., Wezterm, Terminal.app). To set it up, install it via homebrew (by adding it to your Nix configuration or running `brew install herder`). Create a configuration file at `~/.config/herder/config.toml` and optionally add key bindings [1]. Then create a symbolic link for the config directory, rebuild your Nix system (if using Nix), and launch Herder by typing `herder` in your terminal [3].

Then create the configuration directory and a config file at the location `config.toml` [1]. Create a symbolic link for the config directory [3]. After rebuilding your Nix configuration, launch Herder by running the `herdr` command inside your terminal emulator [3]. The video uses Wezterm as the terminal emulator, but any terminal works [4][7].

## Herder configuration file contents

The provided chunks do not directly answer the follow-up query about the specific contents of Herder's config.toml or how to set up key bindings and workspaces. Chunk [s1.1] discusses key bindings in the context of Neovim, not Herder. Chunk [s1.2] explains creating a symbolic link for Wezterm's config directory. Therefore, no explicit guidance on Herder's configuration file contents is available from these chunks.

## Herder integration with agent harnesses (e.g., Claude Code)

The provided chunks discuss terminal multiplexers, agent memory files, and global rules, but do not directly explain how to integrate Herder with specific agent harnesses like Claude Code or set up status lines. [s2.1] mentions the need for managing multiple agent sessions and introduces tmux. [s2.2] and [s2.3] describe setting up a global memory file for all agents, but not Herder-specific integration. Therefore, the follow-up query remains unanswered by these chunks.

## Key Findings

1. Herder is a terminal multiplexer designed for the AI agent era that runs inside a terminal emulator app like WezTerm [1][2].
2. You install Herder via Homebrew as a normal brew formula (not a cask) and configure it with a `config.toml` file [1].
3. Herder provides a left side panel for managing workspaces and agents, plus a main terminal area with tabs and pane splitting [2].
4. Herder has native integration with agent harnesses like Claude Code, displaying real-time status such as model name and context usage [4].

## Finding 1: What Herder Is and What App You Run It In

Herder is a **terminal multiplexer** — a tool that lets you manage multiple terminal sessions, windows, tabs, and panes in one window [1][3]. It is **not a standalone application**. You run it **inside a terminal emulator**. In the demonstration, the creator uses **WezTerm** as his terminal emulator app (installed via Homebrew as a cask) and then launches Herder from within it [1][2]. The creator notes that Herder "might be the only terminal multiplexer that works on Windows as well" [1]. So the answer is: install a terminal emulator like WezTerm (or any other terminal), open it, and then run the `herder` command inside it.

## Finding 2: How to Install Herder

Herder is installed via **Homebrew as a normal brew formula** (not a cask). In the video, the creator adds it to his Nix-based Homebrew configuration by listing it among the brew formulas (separate from casks) [1]. The config file is a `config.toml` placed at a specific configuration directory location, where you set key bindings and other preferences [1][2]. The key bindings shown are custom ones to preserve muscle memory from tmux, but the defaults work fine if you haven't used tmux before [2].

## Finding 3: Herder's Agent-Focused Features

What makes Herder stand out from traditional multiplexers like tmux is that it's "built in this agent era" — it understands what agents are and integrates with mainstream agent harnesses out of the box [1]. When running an agent harness like Claude Code inside Herder, the left side panel automatically detects the agent activity and can display real-time status information such as the model name (e.g., Opus) and context window usage percentage [4]. This works consistently across different agent harnesses, not just Claude Code [4].

## Finding 4: Herder's Interface and Basic Usage

Once you launch Herder inside your terminal emulator, you see a **side panel on the left** that organizes your workspaces and agents, plus a main terminal area [2]. You can create new tabs (and name them), split tabs into multiple panes, and detach/re-attach sessions — similar to what tmux offers [2]. The creator uses Herder to manage multiple agent sessions in parallel, for example launching Claude Code inside a Herder session and then splitting panes to use Neovim and git alongside it to review changes [2][4].

---

**References**

[1] Installing Herder via Homebrew as a normal brew formula, creating `config.toml` for key bindings [video: 5N-okeDdIuI, 34:02–35:23]

[2] Launching Herder inside WezTerm, using side panel, tabs, and panes [video: 5N-okeDdIuI, 35:16–36:47]

[3] Terminal multiplexers explained — managing multiple agent sessions requires them [video: 5N-okeDdIuI, 32:59–34:10]

[4] Herder detecting Claude Code activity and displaying model/context info in the side panel [video: 5N-okeDdIuI, 38:09–39:33]

## Key Findings

1. The Gold Coast is described as a historically "volatile boom and bust market" with extreme vacancy swings from 0.5% to 9% within a typical five-year cycle [1][2].
2. COVID-era migration to the Gold Coast is already reversing as data shows people are "moving home" back to their original cities after 12–18 months [1].
3. The market is seeing a resurgence of off-the-plan "spruikers" and buyer's agent institutes reminiscent of the pre-GFC mid-2000s era, prompting concern it could "get smashed harder than any" [1][2].
4. Off-the-plan purchases carry acute valuation risk, where buyers can be "20% down the day that you've got to settle" because valuations fall during the 3-year construction window [3].
5. On a national scale, the only way to truly collapse the Australian property market would be to "absolutely cut migration to nil" — which is not happening, with 2.4 million migrants expected between 2022–2030 [5].
6. Many Southeast Queensland developers have shelved plans because construction costs make projects unfeasible unless selling at boutique high-end premiums, limiting new supply [6][10].

## Finding 1: Historic Boom-Bust Volatility and Extreme Supply Swings

The Gold Coast has always been a "volatile boom and bust market" driven by its lifestyle and holiday-destination character [1]. The supply cycle is described as extreme — vacancy rates swing from as low as 0.5% to as high as 9% within roughly five years [2][4]. One commentator calls this supply "yo-yo" pattern "brutal" and notes that when supply is tight, buying seems good, but when the pipeline delivers, the market can tip into oversupply almost overnight [2]. The same pattern was observed in inner-city Brisbane's Hamilton precinct, which swung to 9.5% vacancy with developers forced to lease 30 units at a time because they could not sell them [3].

## Finding 2: COVID Migration Reversal Undermining Demand

The COVID-era narrative of city-dwellers permanently relocating to the Gold Coast for work-from-home lifestyles is not holding up in the data. Migration data shows "everyone's moving home" — those who left Melbourne during COVID stayed 12–18 months on the Gold Coast but then returned because they "still have family and obligations there" [1]. This reversal of temporary demand is a risk to the market's current pricing levels, particularly as much of the recent buying was fuelled by that short-lived migration wave [1].

## Finding 3: Spruikers, Off-the-Plan Risks, and GFC Parallels

Commentators draw direct parallels between what is happening now on the Gold Coast and the lead-up to the Global Financial Crisis in the mid-2000s, when "all the penthouses and all the marketing and all the spruikers" emerged [1]. A lot of buyer's agent institutes are again "coming out of the Gold Coast spruiking up prices," leading one expert to state: "I'm concerned. I think that market could get smashed harder than any" [2]. Off-the-plan buyers face acute valuation risk — they commit to a price today for a property completed three years later, and if the market turns, they "can be 20% down the day that you've got to settle," facing deposit loss and negative equity [3][5]. The advice given to clients is to buy "acute resales" in the completed building instead of off-the-plan, because at least then "you know what the market's doing at the time you're buying it" [4].

## Finding 4: National Property Collapse Is Unlikely, but Localised Risk Is Real

At the national level, one expert argues the "only one way to collapse the property market here in this country is to absolutely cut migration to nil" — which is not happening, with 1 million migrants expected 2022–2026 and a further 1.4 million between 2026 and 2030, underpinning housing demand [5][5]. However, localised markets can still experience severe downturns even when the national picture is strong. As the Perth example from earlier cycles showed, markets that have "had long runs of growth" can "tank and take a serious hit" or "flatline for a decade" — Sydney from 2003–2013 went backwards, and Brisbane, Perth, and Adelaide did "nothing" from 2007–2020, even going backwards [9][6]. The Gold Coast, with its boom-bust DNA and current off-the-plan frenzy, is especially vulnerable to such a localised correction [2][1].

## Finding 5: Developer Feasibility Constraints May Limit Oversupply

While the risk of oversupply has historically plagued the Gold Coast, current conditions are different. Many developers in Southeast Queensland — including on the Gold Coast — have "shelved plans" because construction and material costs have made projects unviable unless they sell at boutique high-end premiums [6][10]. Replacement costs are "just way higher than an established property," so unless developers can achieve extreme premiums, "they can't make their margins work" and simply shelve their plans [6][10]. This could paradoxically limit the supply flood that has historically caused the Gold Coast's bust cycles, though it also means fewer new homes are being built to satisfy underlying population-driven demand [6].

I enjoy working end to end transforming stakeholder problems into data driven solutions. I’m pivoting to AI to expand my impact from supporting business performance to building agentic solutions and capture a data driven loop. ""

answers.answer:
I have enough evidence to give you comprehensive, transcript-backed feedback and a revision. Here's what the research reveals about what your summary needs.

## Key Findings

1. Hiring managers spend only ~6 seconds on a resume before deciding, so your summary must hook them instantly with proven impact rather than generic claims [2][4].
2. For career changers, the summary must demonstrate active learning effort in the new discipline — nobody hires for something you've never done without seeing you work to master it [1][2][3].
3. The strongest summaries prove capability with specific facts and figures, making the reader think "wow, you did that for your last employer — I want you to do that for me" [1][2].
4. The best professional summary blends experience, skills, relationship building, and measurable impact while also revealing character [3][5].
5. Numbers and specifics are critical — they help the reader understand exactly what you did and how it helped your employers succeed [3].

---

## Analysis of Your Current Draft

**What works:** Your "10+ years experience shipping measurable impact" line is strong because it signals tenure with proof of delivery. The pivot narrative (data science → AI engineering) is clear.

**What needs fixing:**

| Issue | Why it's a problem |
|---|---|
| "Highly skilled" | Tells instead of shows. Replaces a slot where a specific number or achievement could go [1][2]. |
| No facts or figures anywhere | The #1 rule — you need specific numbers to make the reader think "wow" [1][3]. |
| "I enjoy working end to end" | Passive, personal-taste language. Re-frame as a capability, not a preference. |
| "capture a data driven loop" | Vague and grammatically awkward. Leaves the reader confused. |
| No proof of AI learning effort | For a career pivot, you must show you're actively upskilling — "no one is going to hire you for something you've never done if they don't see effort to learn" [3]. |
| No standout accomplishment anchoring the summary | Leads with "highly skilled" instead of your biggest win [1]. |

---

## Revised Professional Summary (Template — Fill in Your Numbers)

Here is a rewritten version following the transcript-backed guidance. **Bold brackets** are where you insert your specific metrics.

> **Data Scientist → AI Engineer** with 10+ years of delivering **[X%]** revenue lift through **[type of solution, e.g., ML-driven optimization]** across tech, startup, and consulting environments. Led end-to-end delivery of **[Y projects / systems]** that transformed stakeholder problems into production data solutions generating **[$Z in impact / % improvement]**. Now actively pivoting into AI engineering — building **[specific project/course/work product]** to prove out agentic architectures — with the goal of expanding impact from business analytics to building autonomous, data-driven systems that capture a continuous improvement loop.

**Key changes and why (with citations):**

1. **Leads with role + tenure** — tells them immediately who you are [2].
2. **Opens with a specific number achievement** — the hook that makes them think "wow" [1][2].
3. **Replaces "enjoy" with "delivered"** — action language, not preference [2].
4. **Shows active AI learning** — inserts a concrete example of what you're building/learning, which is mandatory for career pivots [1][3].
5. **Clarifies "data driven loop"** — reframed as "continuous improvement loop" inside "autonomous, data-driven systems" so it's concrete and compelling.
6. **Ends with the forward-looking value proposition** — connects past impact to future AI ambition [5].

---

## Optional: A Shorter, Punchier Version

If you prefer something tighter (better for the 6-second scan [2]):

> **AI Engineer (pivoting from Data Science)** | 10+ yrs shipping measurable business impact — **[X% revenue lift / $Y savings]** via end-to-end ML solutions. Currently building **[specific AI project]** to deepen agentic systems expertise. Seeking to apply a proven data-to-impact loop to autonomous AI product development.

---

## What You Need to Fill In

Based on the transcripts, the single most impactful change you can make is adding **specific numbers** [1][3]. Before you use any version above, identify:

- **A specific metric** from your data science work (e.g., "drove 30% cost reduction," "increased conversion by 15%")
- **A concrete AI learning project** you can mention (a course cert, a built agent, a deployed LLM prototype, etc.) — this is critical for the career pivot credibility [3]
- **The # of projects/teams/stakeholders** you've worked with

Plug those in and your summary will go from "tells" to "proves" — which is exactly what gets a resume past the 6-second scan [2].

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
Here is a comprehensive guide on how to structure your resume, what to put in each section, and how to format it all.

---

## Key Findings

1. The overall resume structure should follow this order: Name/Contact Info → Professional Title → Professional Summary → Skills → Work Experience (most recent first) → Education (at the bottom) [1][2][3].
2. Each job entry in the experience section must include the job title (bold), location (italics), company name (regular font), and the *months* of employment — not just the years [1].
3. Bullet points under each role should tell accomplishment stories with numbers, strong action verbs, and varied language — never just list responsibilities [4].
4. The skills section must be curated to pull only skills from the jobs you're targeting, avoiding generic basics like "Microsoft Office" or "attention to detail" [5].
5. Education belongs at the bottom of the resume, should list the full credential name (not just the abbreviation), and should omit graduation years to avoid age discrimination [3].

---

## Finding 1: Overall Resume Section Order — Top to Bottom

The resume flows in a deliberate sequence designed to answer the employer's questions in order. Start with your **name and contact info** (city & state only — no street address to avoid location-based discrimination) [1]. Right below your name, add a **professional title** that defines your brand — something like "Strategic Marketing Director" or "E-commerce SEO Strategist" — covering what you do, your level, and your industry [3]. Next comes the **professional summary** (not an outdated objective statement), which should state what you are, your years of experience, the environments you've worked in, and — by the second sentence — a specific accomplishment [3]. After that, insert your **skills section**, then your **work experience** in reverse-chronological order, and finally **education** at the bottom [1][3].

## Finding 2: How to Structure Each Job Entry in the Experience Section

Each experience entry must be formatted for both ATS scanners and human readers. List jobs from **most recent to least recent** with no exceptions — ATS systems and recruiters both need this order [1]. For each role, the line should present: **your job title in bold** (so they can instantly see what positions you've held), the **location in italics** (to visually differentiate it), and the **company name in regular font** [1]. Crucially, include the **months** you were in the role (e.g., "March 2021 – June 2023"), not just the years. Year-only dates hide whether you were there for two weeks or two years, which makes you look untrustworthy [1].

## Finding 3: How to Write Bullet Points That Sell Your Accomplishments

Bullet points are the most important part of the experience section, and most people write them wrong. Rather than listing what you were *responsible for* (e.g., "responsible for managing the company's online marketing initiatives" — which tells the reader nothing), write bullet points that tell the story of **what you did and how it helped the company succeed** [4]. Strong bullet points: (1) start with a **strong action verb**, (2) include **quantified numbers** where possible (e.g., "38% online revenue increase," "26% improvement in ROI"), and (3) **vary the wording** so you don't sound like everyone else using AI-generated language [4][6]. The difference is dramatic — "oversee a small team" becomes "led a 12-person cross-functional marketing team optimizing paid, organic, and email channels to improve ROI by 26%" [6].

## Finding 4: How to Build a Smart Skills Section

The skills section should sit before your experience, and it must be curated intentionally. Do **not** include basic, entry-level skills like "strong communication," "attention to detail," "Microsoft Office," or "time management" — these waste space and make a seasoned professional look junior [5]. Instead, **pull the skills directly from the job descriptions you are applying to**, selecting only those that are genuinely interesting and relevant to the employer [5]. Format the section compactly using a borderless table (e.g., 3x4 grid) with bullet points for each skill, so it doesn't take up excessive vertical space or leave awkward white space on the page [2].

## Finding 5: Education and Formatting Best Practices

Education is not the most important section — put it **at the bottom of page two** [3]. Write out the **full name of your credential** (e.g., "Bachelor of Arts" not just "BA") for a more professional look, and **do not include the graduation years** — employers can use that to infer your age and discriminate [3]. For overall formatting: use **10-point font** for body text to keep it condensed and professional, adjust margins to avoid single words hanging on a new line, and use the "full justified" alignment to squeeze tight lines together cleanly [5]. Maintain consistent paragraph spacing (e.g., 12pt after each line) and avoid orphans — if a role's bullet points spill to page two, add a "continued" label so content doesn't float disconnected from its context [7].

---

The difference is dramatic — \"oversee a small team\" becomes \"led a 12-person cross-functional marketing team optimizing paid, organic, and email channels to improve ROI by 26%\" [6].\n\n## Finding 4: How to Build a Smart Skills Section\n\nThe skills section should sit before your experience, and it must be curated intentionally. Do **not** include basic, entry-level skills like \"strong communication,\" \"attention to detail,\" \"Microsoft Office,\" or \"time management\" — these waste space and make a seasoned professional look junior [5]. Instead, **pull the skills directly from the job descriptions you are applying to**, selecting only those that are genuinely interesting and relevant to the employer [5]. Format the section compactly using a borderless table (e.g., 3x4 grid) with bullet points for each skill, so it doesn't take up excessive vertical space or leave awkward white space on the page [2].\n\n## Finding 5: Education and Formatting Best Practices\n\nEducation is not the most important section — put it **at the bottom of page two** [3]. Write out the **full name of your credential** (e.g., \"Bachelor of Arts\" not just \"BA\") for a more professional look, and **do not include the graduation years** — employers can use that to infer your age and discriminate [3]. For overall formatting: use **10-point font** for body text to keep it condensed and professional, adjust margins to avoid single words hanging on a new line, and use the \"full justified\" alignment to squeeze tight lines together cleanly [5]. They provide several example approaches: for experienced professionals, state your tenure and strongest skills [5]; for career changers, show that you are actively learning the new field [2]; for new professionals or students, highlight your potential and willingness to grow [2]. A favorite example blends experience, skills, relationship building, and impact while also revealing character [3]. The videos also offer ready-to-use templates with square brackets as placeholders for your own information [3][1]. The second video (owIP4Qr39BY) does not directly address writing the summary content; it focuses on other resume sections and services [4][6].

Kun frames his AI engineering workflow as a \"captain and crew mates\" metaphor, where he acts as the captain orchestrating multiple AI agent sessions in parallel [2][6].\n2. He uses a reproducible environment stack with Nix, nix-darwin, Home Manager, Westerm terminal emulator, and Neovim — all declaratively configured via dotfiles [8][10].\n3. Agent onboarding is done through a two-part memory system: a minimal global memory file (27 lines) for cross-project preferences, and more verbose project-level memory files that accumulate learnings from agent corrections [1][9].\n4. Conditional knowledge is offloaded into \"skills\" with progressive disclosure to avoid bloating system prompts, installed via Vercel's `npx skills` CLI [6][8].\n5. Planning happens through Lavish AXI — a rich editor that generates interactive HTML artifacts for visual requirement clarification, with voice input via Open Super Whisper [2][9].\n6. During implementation, agents work autonomously in isolated git work trees managed by Treehouse, with long-running tasks handled by \"Good Night, Have Fun\" [1][4][7].\n7. Instead of manually reviewing diffs, Kun sends changes into the \"No Mistakes\" pipeline, which performs adversarial review, end-to-end testing with evidence capture, documentation updates, linting, and PR babysitting [3][4][1].\n8. For scaling beyond manual session management, Kun built \"First Mate\" — an orchestrator agent that accepts high-level goals, spawns parallel agent sessions in T-Max/Herder tabs, and manages the full build-validate-PR lifecycle autonomously [5][6][9].\n\n## Finding 1: Reproducible Environment Stack\nKun's entire development environment is declaratively configured for full reproducibility. On a fresh Mac, he uses the Determinate Nix installer to set up Nix, then configures macOS-level settings via nix-darwin and user-level settings via Home Manager, with Homebrew installed as a Nix package [2][8]. The terminal emulator is Westerm — chosen for being truly cross-platform (identical on Windows, Mac, Linux) and highly customizable through Lua scripts with hot-reload [1][6][7]. Inside Westerm, he runs a terminal multiplexer: originally T-Max, but more recently switching to Herder which he describes as \"built in this agent era\" with native integration for agent harnesses [3][4]. His primary code editor is Neovim, configured with Lua and managed via the Lazy plugin manager, with plugins like Which-Key for discoverable keybindings [5][7][9]. The shell prompt is customized with Starship, and Zsh is configured with auto-suggestions and syntax highlighting — all managed through the Nix/home-manager config [5][7]. On rebuild, the entire setup is instantly reproducible from a single cloned dotfiles repo [4][5].\n\n## Finding 2: Agent Harnesses and Onboarding (Memory Files + Skills)\nKun keeps his workflow agent-agnostic and uses four different agent harnesses regularly: Claude Code (best out-of-box experience, practical for Anthropic subscriptions), Codex CLI (written in Rust, smoother, open source), Pi coding agent (minimal and highly extensible), and Open Code (buttery smooth TUI, model agnostic) [7][8]. New agents are \"fresh recruits\" that need onboarding through memory files and skills [1][9]. The global memory file (agents.md symlinked to claude.md and other agent locations) is deliberately minimal — only ~27 lines — containing personal preferences like \"never use mdash\" and \"when making technical decisions, don't give too much weight to development cost\" [2][9]. Each project also has a project-level memory file built organically: every time Kun sees an agent making a mistake, he corrects it and asks the agent to store the learning into this file, so agents get \"smarter and more experienced\" over time [7][9]. To prevent memory files from bloating, conditional information (like end-to-end testing instructions) is extracted into skills with progressive disclosure — only a tiny description field loads into the system prompt initially, and the full content loads only when the skill is activated [6][8][10]. Skills are managed via `npx skills` CLI from Vercel, and Kun warns strongly against installing random skills from the internet due to security risks and unverified performance claims [6][8].\n\n## Finding 3: Planning Phase — Lavish AXI with Voice Input\nFor planning any complex work, Kun relies on Lavish AXI — a custom tool that instructs the agent to generate interactive HTML artifacts that visualize what needs to be discussed, always using the same design system as the current project [2][9]. He describes this as \"so much easier to understand than the huge wall of text\" and states he \"can never go back to reading text in the terminal anymore\" [1][9]. The Lavish editor allows him to annotate and comment on specific parts of artifacts to give feedback, and at the bottom there are interactive decision options he can click to make choices — all without leaving the Lavish interface [9]. For input, he uses Open Super Whisper for local voice transcription, only falling back to typing for URLs and file paths [5][9]. Once requirements are clarified in this planning phase, he tells the agent to \"start building\" and exits the session, confident that the implementation phase will run autonomously [1][9].\n\n## Finding 4: Implementation Phase — Parallel Autonomous Agent Sessions\nAfter planning, Kun does not interfere during implementation — \"I only come back to this when the agent has done\" [1][9]. To run multiple agents in parallel without conflicts, he uses Treehouse — a tool he built that manages git work trees (lightweight isolated copies of the repo). Running `treehouse` drops him into a fresh work tree, he can spin up many of them, and when done, closing the tab frees the work tree for reuse instead of creating new ones each time [4][7]. For long-running autonomous tasks (e.g., overnight), he uses \"Good Night, Have Fun\" — another free open-source tool that keeps an agent running in a loop until a stop condition (token cap, iteration cap, etc.) is met. He gives an example of telling it to \"pretend you are a seven-year-old kid and use the app end to end, find the first usability problem, fix it, and repeat\" — and the agent keeps iterating autonomously [1][2][3]. He uses T-Max (or Herder) tabs to run all these parallel agent sessions, switching between them with keyboard shortcuts and monitoring their status via the top status bar [4][7][9].\n\n## Finding 5: Validation and PR Pipeline — \"No Mistakes\"\nKun's core insight is that manually reviewing diffs creates a bottleneck because \"AI writes code so fast\" and \"reviewing diff is just not fun\" [3][9]. Instead, he sends changes into a pipeline he built called \"No Mistakes\" (free and open source) [2][3]. The pipeline executes in an isolated work tree so nothing affects the current repo. It first analyzes the agent session to understand the real intent, then rebases on the latest main branch and resolves merge conflicts upfront [1][3]. Next, it runs an adversarial review in its own fresh context window — \"this is where most problems get caught\" — with obvious problems self-corrected and ambiguous ones escalated to the human for a product decision [1][4]. After review, it does end-to-end testing against the original intent, recording evidence (screenshots, video demos, log files) that proves the change is working [3][4]. It then updates all relevant documentation and checks for linting problems before pushing the branch and raising a PR [1][4]. Crucially, No Mistakes continues \"babysitting\" the PR until it's merged — handling merge conflicts and CI pipeline failures autonomously [1][4]. Kun's review process is then risk-based: he looks at the risk assessment on the PR, and for low-risk changes doesn't review the diff at all, relying on the pipeline's evidence [3][6].\n\n## Finding 6: First Mate — The Orchestrator for True Scale\nKun discovered that even with parallelized agent sessions, \"juggling between all these sessions... the constant context switch\" was exhausting [6][9]. His solution is \"First Mate\" — another free open-source tool — an orchestrator agent that acts as the captain's primary interface. He talks to First Mate and gives it high-level goals like \"for all three projects, I'd like to add an update command on the CLI that will update their version to the latest on npm\" [7][9]. First Mate realizes this is three parallel tasks, spins up T-Max/Herder tabs, creates Treehouse work trees, runs agents in those work trees, and runs No Mistakes to validate and get PRs ready — all autonomously [6][9][10]. While waiting for those background tasks, Kun can give First Mate additional work like \"look at the most recent three open issues\" — First Mate pulls the issues while agents are still running in the background [6][9]. He describes watching First Mate context-switch as \"an oddly satisfying experience\" [9][10]. This final layer transforms Kun from someone managing many agents directly into a true captain focused on \"big picture stuff like where should we go next\" [6][9].\n\n## Finding 7: Efficient Agent Tool Design (AXI Standards) and Tool Selection\nKun is meticulous about tool efficiency for agents. He authored \"AXI\" — a set of design standards for building tools that treat agents as first-class citizens, optimizing for \"agent ergonomics.\" For example, using token-efficient output formats can save ~40% tokens compared to JSON [1][2]. He benchmarked various ways to access GitHub and found that the GitHub MCP server costs \"three times more on token cost and more than double the latency\" compared to using the CLI, while his GitHub AXI achieved the lowest cost and highest success rate [2]. He built custom AXI tools including GitHub AXI, Chrome DevTools AXI (benchmarked against various browser tools), and Lavish AXI for planning [2][9]. All AXI tools are available on axi.md with a public catalog, and he warns against using unverified tools: he tested the popular \"Andrej Karpathy skills\" repo (177k stars) with Program Bench and found it used 5% more tokens while making results worse — and notes it wasn't even written by Karpathy himself [6][8].",

conversations.question: What are the key tax changes affecting property investors right now?

answers.title: rag_llm (single-hop)
answers.answer: The key tax changes include: (1) Negative gearing limitations for newly purchased existing properties, with a transitional period until July 2028 before cash flow impact [1][10]; (2) Capital gains tax (CGT) changes requiring market value assessments for existing properties as of 1 July 2027, with a 50% CGT calculation on the gain up to that value and indexation beyond [7]; (3) A new 30% flat trust tax on trustees and potential double taxation on distributions to corporate beneficiaries (bucket companies) [7]; (4) A minimum 30% tax rate on capital gains regardless of the investor's marginal tax bracket [7]; (5) Grandfathering of existing properties, meaning investors are advised not to sell grandfathered assets to maximize tax benefits [1][4]. answers.answer:
**Key tax changes for property investors:** Negative gearing on existing residential properties will be restricted: for properties held before the budget, a 50% CGT calculation to market value as of 1 July 2027 followed by indexation [7]; properties purchased after the budget still receive full negative gearing until the July 2028 tax return [10]. A minimum 30% tax rate on capital gains applies regardless of marginal tax bracket [7]. Trust tax changes: trustees face a flat 30% tax, and distributions to corporate beneficiaries (bucket companies) may cause double taxation [7]. These changes hit mom-and-dad investors hardest, while sophisticated investors can use company structures to mitigate [2][9]; overall, reduced investment demand may increase rents [9].

### Trust tax double taxation
The provided chunks describe the trust tax changes as having a 'very minimal' impact overall [s1.4][s1.7]. The flat 30% trustee tax effectively raises the minimum tax rate on trust income, reducing the benefit of distributing to lower-income beneficiaries. Distributions to corporate beneficiaries (bucket companies) may incur double taxation, but the precise mechanics are not detailed. Trusts still remain viable, especially when used as shareholders of companies to distribute fully franked dividends [s1.8]. For sophisticated investors, using companies may become more attractive [s1.9]. The evidence does not provide a step-by-step application for family trusts; it mainly notes that trusts become 'a little bit less attractive' [s1.8][s1.9].

### Minimum CGT rate interaction with 50% discount
The retrieved chunks do not explicitly answer whether the minimum 30% CGT rate replaces or applies after the 50% discount. One source states that investors with income $45,000 or below will pay 30% tax on the 'real gain', which could be interpreted as the gain after the 50% discount, but this is not clarified [s2.1]. No further detail is provided in the available evidence.

I now have comprehensive evidence. Let me compile my final answer.

## Key Findings
1. Negative gearing is being phased out for existing residential properties from 1 July 2027 and will only be available for new properties thereafter, while pre-budget holdings are fully grandfathered [1][3].
2. The CGT regime is shifting to an indexation method (abolished in 1999), requiring a market valuation at 1 July 2027, with a 50% discount applying up to that date and indexation thereafter [1][4].
3. A new minimum 30% tax rate on real capital gains applies regardless of an investor's marginal tax bracket, hitting low-income investors earning $45,000 or below the hardest [1][7].
4. Trustees are being taxed at a flat 30%, effectively removing the ability to distribute income to lower-tax-rate beneficiaries, and distributions to corporate beneficiaries may face double taxation [1][7].
5. The changes overwhelmingly impact "mom and dad" investors (92% of investors own two or fewer properties) while sophisticated investors using structures like companies can largely adapt [3][6].
6. Properties held pre-budget are grandfathered under the old rules which strongly disincentivizes selling — investors report they will hold these assets longer, reducing overall stock [1][4][9].

## Finding 1: Negative Gearing Phase-Out for Existing Properties
Properties owned before budget night (12 May, 7:30pm) retain their negative gearing benefits indefinitely under grandfathering provisions [3]. However, for any property purchased after budget night, negative gearing is available only until 1 July 2027, after which it is restricted exclusively to newly built properties [1][3]. The stated government intent is to redirect investment toward new housing supply, with one expert describing it as a "white flag" admission that "we're just not building enough property" [1]. For a typical investor at a 30% tax rate who was negatively geared by $20,000 a year, this means losing a $6,000 annual tax refund — the shortfall is quarantined and carried forward to offset future capital gains [2].

## Finding 2: Capital Gains Tax Moves to Indexation
The budget reintroduces the indexation method for CGT, which was originally abolished in September 1999 [4]. All properties (excluding brand-new ones built after the budget) must obtain a market valuation as at 1 July 2027 — a 50% CGT discount applies up to that date, and then an indexed cost-base method applies thereafter [1][4]. The indexation method was previously considered an "unproductive tax" because it incentivized holding assets even during stagnation, as the inflating cost base reduced tax payable [4]. Additionally, a minimum 30% tax rate applies to the real capital gain regardless of the investor's marginal tax bracket, meaning someone earning $45,000 or less will still pay 30% CGT — described as "nasty for any spouses that may not be working or younger people wanting to invest on lower incomes" [1][7].

## Finding 3: Trust Tax Flat Rate and Double Taxation Risks
Trustees are now subject to a flat 30% tax rate, removing the previous strategy of distributing income to beneficiaries on lower marginal tax rates to minimise overall tax [1][7]. Furthermore, distributions to corporate beneficiaries (commonly known as "bucket companies") may attract an additional tax, creating the risk of double taxation [7]. One accountant notes, "My game has changed... I no longer play in the realms of 0 to 47%. We may be playing in the realms of 30 to 47" [2]. For early-stage investors buying in their own name, the advice is that the game hasn't changed significantly, but more sophisticated investors now need to consider incorporating companies as part of their investment structure [2].

## Finding 4: Disproportionate Impact on Mom-and-Dad Investors
The consensus across all sources is that the changes most heavily affect small-scale investors — "mom and dad investors, your young Aussies who are rent vesting that scrimped and saved to have one place" [3][6]. Sophisticated investors using trusts and company structures are described as being able to "take them or leave them" because they were already foregoing some negative gearing benefits or not getting the full 50% CGT discount [3]. One analyst quantified the difference: for a high-bracket investor making a $1 million gain, the changes represent roughly an extra $65,000 in tax — "I'm not going to invest because I pay an extra $65,000 in tax for a million bucks" [5]. However, 92% of Australian property investors own two or fewer properties, meaning the vast majority are in the heavily impacted camp [3].

## Finding 5: Grandfathering Incentivises Holding, Reducing Stock
Properties owned before budget night are fully grandfathered under the old negative gearing and CGT rules, which creates a powerful disincentive to sell [1][4]. One experienced investor states plainly: "We won't sell any of our properties which are grandfathered" and "you'd be really stupid to sell your grandfather properties" [1][9]. The strategy for these investors is to maintain and maximise debt on grandfathered properties (to continue claiming negative gearing) while paying down debt on any new assets they buy [4]. This is expected to reduce stock turnover in established areas, potentially worsening supply constraints [9]. One commentator notes that properties will need to be held for longer periods for the indexation method to be beneficial — it "isn't great for short-term bursts and maybe sales after 3 or 4 years" [2].

## Finding 6: Commercial Property and Superannuation Unaffected
Negative gearing for commercial property remains unchanged under the budget — investors can still claim it on commercial assets, though the panellists note that "you're not buying commercial property for the purpose of negative gearing" [2]. Within superannuation, the 1/3 capital gains discount still applies, and with the super fund's 15% tax rate, the effective tax rate on a gain is roughly 10% [5]. Some sophisticated investors are becoming more "transactive" inside super — buying assets, capturing growth, selling, paying the roughly 10% tax, and reinvesting into the next property — a strategy that can result in zero tax if assets are held until retirement in the pension phase [5].

The key tax changes affecting property investors are the **removal of negative gearing for new purchases of existing residential property**, **tightened capital gains tax (CGT) rules**, and a **new 30% flat trust tax** that also hits bucket‑company distributions. Existing investors are grandfathered, but new buyers will feel the cash‑flow pinch from mid‑2028.

- **Negative‑gearing removal:** Investors can no longer claim rental losses on existing properties bought after the budget, which disincentivises buying and is expected to withdraw 10–20% of investor buyers [g11][g12][g21]. Serviceability drops by 20% without negative gearing [g26], and the change takes effect for tax returns filed from July 2028 onwards [10]. Grandfathered properties retain their benefits [1].

- **Capital gains tax changes:** From 1 July 2027, all properties (except brand‑new builds) will require a market valuation, with a 50% CGT calculation up to that date and indexation thereafter [7]. A **minimum 30% tax rate on real capital gains** applies regardless of the investor’s marginal tax bracket, hitting lower‑income spouses and younger investors hardest [7].

- **Trust tax:** Trustees will pay a **flat 30% tax** on distributions, removing the ability to stream income to lower‑tax beneficiaries. Distributions to corporate beneficiaries (bucket companies) may face double taxation [7].

- **Timeline and response:** The full cash‑flow impact arrives in July 2028, about 25 months after the budget [10]. Sophisticated investors are buying now at discounted prices (5–10% lower) and expecting rents to rise $100–200/week within 12–24 months to bridge the gap [g14][9]. Mom‑and‑dad investors are being driven toward new‑build stock [g1].

## Key Themes Overview

The corpus contains three distinct themes: (1) Agentic engineering workflow for coding, including terminal‑centric setup, agent onboarding via memory files and skills, and managing multiple agents [1][2][3][5][8][9]; (2) Australian property market and budget discussions, covering monthly data reviews and owner‑occupier appeal [4][10]; (3) Resume writing professional summaries, with examples and templates for job seekers [6][7].

## Memory files and skills setup for agent onboarding

Kun configures global and project‑level memory files as follows: He creates a central global memory file (e.g., `/home/agents.md`) that is symlinked into each agent's directory, ensuring all agents load the same rules via Home Manager distribution [s1.1][s1.4]. The global file is minimal (~27 lines) to save tokens and includes personal preferences such as avoiding em dashes and not overvaluing development cost [s1.3]. For each project, a project‑level memory file (e.g., `claude.md` or `agents.md`) is stored similarly, containing project context, layout, terminology, and collective learning from past agent interactions [s1.2][s1.5]. He builds this iteratively by correcting agent mistakes and asking it to remember the lesson [s1.2]. To reduce bloat, conditionally useful instructions are extracted from memory files into skills using a skill creator tool [s1.6]. The entire configuration is reproducible via a file repo that can be rebuilt from a fresh Mac [s1.7][s1.8].

In the monthly data release, key changes across Australian capital cities include: Over the past year, most markets picked up, with Darwin and Perth as 'high flyers', while Canberra, Melbourne, Sydney lagged [s2.1]. answers.answer:
I now have enough evidence across all the videos to answer comprehensively. Here is my analysis:

## Key Findings
1. The corpus spans three distinct, unrelated content areas: AI agentic engineering, Australian property market and tax policy analysis, and resume writing and career development.
2. AI agentic engineering content, presented by former Meta/Atlassian principal engineer Kun, focuses on building production-grade AI coding workflows with memory files, skills, and automated PR pipelines [1][6].
3. Australian property content analyzes the federal budget's impact on negative gearing, capital gains tax indexation, and trust taxes, with predictions of a rental crisis and market reset [1][2].
4. Resume writing content provides step-by-step guidance on professional summaries, ATS keyword optimization, formatting, and bullet point construction to secure more job interviews [2][5].

## Finding 1: AI Agentic Engineering — Production-Grade Coding Agents

The AI agentic engineering theme, presented by Kun (a former L8 principal engineer at Meta, Microsoft, and Atlassian), covers practical workflows for using AI coding agents to ship 40–50 production PRs daily [1][6]. The core concepts include setting up global memory files (e.g., `agents.md`) that unify behavior across multiple agent harnesses like Claude Code, Open Code, and Cursor [5], and using "skills" for progressive disclosure — where only a description is loaded into the system prompt and the full file is read only when the agent needs it, preventing token waste [4]. The workflow emphasizes thinking of oneself as an engineering director who sets culture and processes rather than reviewing every diff, and uses an open-source pipeline called "no mistakes" that handles adversarial review, end-to-end testing, documentation updates, and PR babysitting autonomously [1][3].

## Finding 2: Australian Property Market — Federal Budget and Tax Policy Overhaul

A substantial portion of the corpus analyzes the Australian federal budget's four key tax changes: negative gearing reform (limited to new properties only from July 2027), capital gains tax indexation (reintroducing a method abolished in 1999), trust and "bucket company" tax changes (30% flat tax on trustees), and the working Australian's tax offset [1][4]. Experts argue these changes primarily hurt "mom and dad" investors and young Australians rent-vesting, while sophisticated investors using company structures are less affected [2]. The predicted consequences include a massive tightening of rental supply as investors exit existing properties, driving vacancy rates even lower (already at 0.3% in Darwin, 0.6% in Hobart) and pushing rents higher until established properties become cash-flow positive again [3][7].

## Finding 3: Australian Property Market — Market Cycles and Regional Divergence

Multiple videos discuss the cyclical nature of Australian property markets, noting that Sydney went backwards from 2003–2013, and Brisbane, Perth, and Adelaide did nothing from 2007–2020 [7]. Current data shows strong divergence: Darwin, Perth, and Brisbane are high-flyers while Melbourne and Sydney lag, with some affluent Sydney suburbs seeing price drops from sentiment while lower socioeconomic areas see price increases [6][5]. Housing supply has lifted slightly and days on market have increased about 6% across most capitals (from ~34 to ~39 days), but vacancy rates remain extremely tight nationwide [9][4]. The 5% deposit scheme is criticized for pushing young Australians into negative equity in oversupplied areas, particularly in Melbourne and Sydney unit markets [1][2].

## Finding 4: Resume Writing — Professional Summaries and ATS Optimization

The resume writing content emphasizes replacing outdated objective statements with compelling professional summaries, as hiring managers spend only ~6 seconds scanning a resume [2][5]. Multiple formats are provided: a "highlight reel" summary with quantified accomplishments, a career-changer summary demonstrating active learning in the new field, and a new professional summary showcasing potential [1][3]. A key strategy is keyword optimization for Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) — using AI to extract 25 key hard skills from a job description, adding them to the skills section, and then integrating them as bolded headers within bullet points to prove competency to both the ATS and the human reader [3][1].

## Finding 5: Resume Writing — Formatting, Bullet Points, and Anti-Discrimination

Practical formatting advice includes removing street addresses and birth-year email addresses to prevent discrimination, omitting graduation years to avoid age bias, using 10-point body font, removing borders from skills tables, and ensuring consistent spacing [5][3][1]. Bullet points should always start with strong action verbs, include numbers where possible, vary wording to stand out from AI-generated content, and tell a complete story of how the work helped the company succeed [1][6]. The experience section must be ordered most-recent-first, and two-page resumes are acceptable for experienced professionals but not for students [4].

The corpus is split between two main domains: **Australian housing policy and property market commentary** (communities c1, c2, c4, c5, c6, c11) and **technical content on developer tooling, AI‑agent workflows, and environment configuration** (c3, c8, c9, c10, c12), with a smaller but distinct stream on **resume optimization** (c7). Across the property communities there is some disagreement about the causes of rent increases and the ultimate effect of tax changes. The developer communities consistently advocate for progressive disclosure, automated pipelines, and delegating to agent orchestrators.

**Main themes (compact list):**  

1. **Australian housing policy & tax reform** – Negative gearing, CGT changes, and government schemes (e.g., 5% deposit) are predicted to shift investor behavior, potentially raising rents and causing negative equity for young buyers [c1, c5, c6, c11].  
2. **Rental market tightness & supply constraints** – Vacancy rates remain low in several capitals; rising material/labour costs and government policies are seen as limiting new supply [c2, c6, c11].  
3. **Property investment vs. alternative assets** – Residential property is debated as a retirement income vehicle, with some pivoting to REITs, shares, and commercial property in the pension phase [c4].  
4. **Agentic engineering & AI‑driven development** – Workflows emphasise progressive disclosure of skills, automated pipelines (branch, commit, merge), and using orchestrators like “First Mate” to manage multi‑agent projects [c3, c8, c10].  
5. **Developer environment configuration** – Neovim keymaps/plugins, Nix Darwin/home‑manager, and Claude Code status monitoring are repeatedly detailed for setting up reproducible, efficient coding setups [c9, c12].  
6. **Resume optimisation for ATS** – Tactics include keyword extraction from job descriptions, weaving keywords into bullet points, and formatting to survive the “6‑second” human review [c7].  
7. **Disagreement on rent increase causes** – One community attributes rent rises to investor exodus from policy changes [c1]; another argues landlords are not at fault and rents rise from natural market pressure [c11].
