Community summary [c1]: Proposed tax changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax (CGT) exemptions are predicted to push investors toward land estates and new builds on city fringes and highrises, while the removal of negative gearing on existing residential properties is expected to reduce investor activity, increase rents, and decimate the lower class. The short-term supply deficit will be met by new builds, but labor, debt, and material costs have already decreased new build supply, and the government housing model is said to reduce rental supply further. A recurring argument dismisses the idea that removing negative gearing will turn renters into first home buyers, citing that renters will face higher rents and deposit schemes will push property markets up. Citing New Zealand's backtrack on negative gearing reform between 2023 and 2025, the claims suggest a similar U-turn is possible, with a window of opportunity in the next six months before rents rise and policies take effect in 2027 tax returns.

Community summary [c2]: Tight rental markets persist in Darwin, Brisbane, Hobart, Adelaide, and Perth, while days on market have risen in Hobart, Sydney, Canberra, and Melbourne and stock-on-market percentages have increased everywhere. Prices have gone backwards in Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra, and Adelaide, with Brisbane, Perth, and Adelaide having stagnated from 2007 to 2020, though Perth saw rents surge 30–40% annually from population growth in 2023. Market cycle timing is cited as creating opportunities in Sydney, Melbourne, and Canberra, where DSR 3 scores are improving, and Perth’s cycle timing is the third lowest behind Brisbane and Adelaide. Specific local conditions include Docklands in Melbourne likely having high unit stock due to off-the-plan listings, and stock-on-market can exceed 100% in greenfield estates or new suburbs.

Community summary [c3]: This cluster focuses on AI agent–driven software development workflows, emphasizing a **no mistakes pipeline** that automates branching, committing, rebasing on the latest `main branch`, resolving `merge conflicts`, and handling `CI pipeline` failures until a PR merges. Skills employ **progressive disclosure** to keep only the `description field` in the `system prompt` until needed, while **global and project level memory files** store recurring and project-specific knowledge. A recurring argument is that `agents` trained on `human` estimations overvalue **development cost**, producing **cheap solutions** that fail to scale; by contrast, careful **planning phase** clarification lets the agent work without interference during **implementation phase**. Over time, the focus shifts from pipeline mechanics (June 20) to critiquing this bias and recording environment setup (e.g., installing `Chrome`, `Git`, and `SSH key` for `GitHub` on July 5), together with tools like the `skill creator` that teaches the agent to build new skills.

Community summary [c4]: This community focuses on Australian property investing and superannuation strategies, with a strong debate over residential property versus alternatives like shares, REITs, and commercial property. Proponents initially use self-managed super funds (SMSFs) to buy investment properties with high leverage (90% loans, interest-only) and exploit tax benefits such as the 50% capital gains discount and 15% super tax rate, aiming for passive income and retirement goals like the age 60 target. However, by mid-2026, a clear shift emerges: in the pension phase, clients pivot away from residential property toward REITs, shares, cash at bank, and commercial property, as residential property is deemed the “worst producing income vehicle in retirement.” Claims also note that equities and crypto investors look to property as an alternative, while others caution that investment properties, shares, and businesses are “at risk,” and recommend using cash from sales, super, and debt reduction with a financial planner to secure a future passive income. The narrative contrasts a deliberate, long-term property plan (with a 2028 milestone) against a later retreat to more liquid, higher-yielding assets in retirement.

Community summary [c5]: The community revolves around the Australian government’s proposed capital gains tax (CGT) reforms, debated in the context of the 2026 budget and scheduled for implementation by 1 July 2027. Key arguments pit a flat 30% CGT rate — which would impose an extra $65,000 tax on a $1 million gain relative to the existing 50% exemption — against the indexation method that Peter Costello and John Howard abolished in September 1999. Opponents, including Angus Taylor and Pauline Hanson, are portrayed as blocking income tax cuts, while TikTok posts heavily criticize the budget’s economic modeling for discouraging younger investors and owner-occupied demand. The market initially calmed after budget night, but bracket creep from unindexed tax brackets and the prospect of a 30% tax on real gain for all established properties (grandfathered until July 2028) remain contentious, with the Senate inquiry committee set to begin review on 22 June 2026.

Community summary [c6]: The community centers on Australia’s housing market, criticizing government policies that incentivize property spruers through schemes like the 5% deposit scheme and stimulus for off-the-plan purchases and house-and-land packages. Young Australians using the 5% deposit scheme in areas such as Paramea risk negative equity after 15 years, and by March 31, 2026, the scheme’s coverage had dropped to 39% of suburbs. The government is portrayed as shifting responsibility for rental housing to “mom and dad Australian” investors via tax incentives, while neglecting supply-and-demand distortions from divorces and young people. Tax measures—negative gearing, indexation and capital gains tax changes, bucket company rules, and the working Australian’s tax offset—are debated alongside comparisons to France’s cash-gift tax and the heavy reliance of state revenue on stamp duty, second only to the resources industry. Experts like Chris Lawless warn that negative equity, affecting young Australians in oversupplied areas, is nearly as dire as bankruptcy.

Community summary [c7]: This cluster of the corpus revolves around resume optimization to survive the initial 6-second review by hiring managers and pass ATS scanners. Earlier claims emphasize the brevity of human scrutiny (2024), while later ones (2026) provide detailed tactics: using ChatGPT with a keyword optimization prompt to extract top 25 keywords from the job description, tying resume bullet points to those keywords, and adding bold titles to each bullet point. Formatting advice shifts over time to include 10-point font for body text and a border feature for underlining titles, alongside upgrading bullet points with real stories and impact metrics rather than just facts and figures. The recurring argument is that keyword stuffing a key skills section alone is insufficient; instead, keywords must be woven into bullet points and body text, with a free resume writing course on YouTube promoted as a comprehensive resource. Concrete entities like ATS scanner, ChatGPT, bold titles, and the 6-second window define this community’s focus on bridging the gap between automated filters and human decision-makers.

Community summary [c8]: This community focuses on practical workflows and tooling around Anthropic's Claude Code, with Dario (Anthropic's CEO) mentioned in passing. Users customize the status line in Cloud Code to monitor the model (e.g., opus 4.8) and context window usage, and the /status command was introduced for that purpose. Herder emerges as a cross-agent harness solution for consistent status tracking, while Lavish provides a browser-based rich editor and skills are automatically invoked by Claude. Recurring concerns include managing the weekly quota—setting goals before bed risks depletion—and automating commit messages with Claude as co-author. No major temporal shift is evident; the claims from June and July 2026 show incremental refinement of monitoring and the integration of Herder.

Community summary [c9]: This community centers on configuring Neovim, focusing on keybindings, plugin management, and navigation. The configuration involves installing and managing plugins like Lazy, which-key, and snacks via a dedicated plugins directory and init.lua, with Folke noted as the author of both Lazy and which-key. Keybindings are emphasized: ESC exits insert mode, the leader key and space key (e.g., space F) launch tools like neoit and the file picker, and relative line numbers enable jumps (e.g., 11K). Earlier claims (June 2026) cover basic modes and relative line numbering, while later ones (July 2026) detail plugin setup—such as creating navigation.lua to install snacks and setting Lazy to false to disable lazy loading—showing a shift from fundamentals to specific configuration decisions for the Neovim environment.

Community summary [c10]: This cluster centers on the First Mate tool as a productivity layer for managing agent sessions across multiple projects—Lavish AXI, GitHub AXI, Chrome DevTools AXI—by spinning up tabs in T‑Max and pulling actionable issues (e.g., issue 87 from the lavish axi repo). Speakers advocate a mindset shift from micromanaging individual agents to focusing on user understanding and crafting a “treasure map” to guide the crew (captain / sailor metaphor), with Codeex CLI (written in Rust) enabling the ecosystem. The recurring position is that delegating to First Mate eliminates the bottleneck of talking to each agent session one by one, while T‑Max is noted as lacking a tab bar and metadata by default—addressing these through First Mate’s tabs is presented as a significant improvement to developer velocity.

Community summary [c11]: This community centers on the Australian housing market in mid-2026, where federal budget policies—including negative gearing changes, CGT changes, and partial grandfathering of old rules until July 2026—are seen as hurting property investors while the government aims to balance first-time home buyers and investors. Rising population is identified as the biggest pressure, with insufficient housing construction driving property prices higher and making cost-to-build (including materials and taxes) a key factor. Landlords are not blamed for rent increases, which are attributed to natural market pressure, and removing population from the market is predicted to cause its decline. The scenario is defined by high interest rates and a market sentiment focused on the tension between investors, tenants, and first-time buyers, with taxes and governments consistently portrayed as taking money.

Community summary [c12]: The cluster revolves around configuring a development environment using **home-manager** and **Nix Darwin**, where home-manager manages the **home directory** and user-level settings (e.g., installing **hack nerd font**, enabling **syntax highlighting**, **auto-suggestions** with **ghost text** based on **command history**), while Nix Darwin handles macOS-level settings. A recurring argument contrasts these tools, with home-manager also used to distribute a **global memory file** to all **agents**, while **project level skills** are extracted from **end to end testing instructions** to reduce file size—echoing a common pattern of offloading conditional information into skills. Earlier claims (June 2026) dwell on agent limitations for **complex tasks** and a deliberate preference to “never use **mdash**” despite **AI models** being trained to use it; later claims (July 2026) shift to concrete **WezTerm** customizations like **window background opacity** and **blur**, and shell improvements such as **ctrl-f-binding** and **starship** prompt configuration via **flake.nix**.

Now I have enough evidence. Let me compile the final answer.

## Key Findings
1. In early June, the KTG Property Podcast labelled the budget changes a "tax grab" and "massive spanner," describing consumer sentiment at levels not seen since COVID and the GFC [4][8].
2. By mid-June, the Smart Property Investment Show pivoted to correcting widespread misconceptions — chief among them that "negative gearing is gone" — and emphasised the 25-month delay before actual impact in July 2028 [2][3][5].
3. By late June, the same network's episode with Sammy Gordon adopted a markedly calmer tone, declaring "the market has calmed a little bit" and that for sophisticated investors "it really changes very little" [3][10].
4. Sophisticated investors were consistently advised not to sell grandfathered properties and instead to pay down debt on new acquisitions, while a shift toward commercial property emerged as a recurring strategic response [1][3][6].
5. The Suburb Data podcast took a data-driven approach throughout June, noting days on market had risen ~6% post-budget but still remained "very tight" across all capital cities — evidence the market had not yet materially cracked [3].
6. Multiple channels pointed to the New Zealand precedent (negative gearing removed in 2022, reinstated in 2024) as grounds for believing Australia's changes might also be short-lived [9][5][8].

## Finding 1: Early June — Shock and criticism from the KTG Property Podcast
Recorded in early June (roughly three weeks after the 12 May budget), the KTG Property Podcast struck the most alarmed tone of any channel studied. Host KTG opened by declaring "there has been a massive spanner thrown in the works for property investors everywhere" and Jeremy Izzaly, a property accountant, repeatedly called the package "definitely a tax grab" that would not "help the property market" [3][8]. They cited consumer sentiment data sitting in the "low 80s, high 70s" — on par with COVID and the Global Financial Crisis — and noted the 22nd of June as the date when the Senate inquiry would begin seriously debating the legislation [1][4]. Despite the alarm, the episode already pivoted to strategy: the strongest advice was not to sell grandfathered properties ("you'd be really stupid to sell your grandfather properties") and instead to redirect capital toward paying down debt on any new post-budget acquisitions [1][6].

## Finding 2: Mid-June — Misconception-busting on the Smart Property Investment Show with Arjent Pal
In what appears to be the next chronological episode, SPI host Liam Gin brought in Arjent Pal (CEO of Investor Kit) for what they described as a "rapid fire" budget debrief [1]. The entire focus was correcting misinformation. Pal's first point was blunt: "Negative gearing is gone. No, it isn't" [2]. He walked through the actual timeline — a property bought in June 2026 would still get full negative gearing on the July 2027 tax return, with the real impact only hitting in July 2028, or "25 months" away [3]. He drew a crucial distinction between "deferred versus gone," explaining that negative gearing losses simply pile up and are later offset against capital gains on sale [4]. The central insight was that "sophisticated property investors" could "take [the changes] or leave them," while the real burden would fall on "mom and dad investors" and young rent-vesters with one or two properties [8].

## Finding 3: Late June — Calming and adaptation with Sammy Gordon on the SPI Show
Later in June, the same SPI network aired an episode titled "The End of the Old Property Playbook?" with high-profile investor Sammy Gordon [2]. The tone had shifted markedly. Gordon stated outright that "I think the market has calmed a little bit since what budget night was" and that "I don't think it changes too much overall in the overall strategy" [3][10]. For sophisticated and advanced investors, he said, "it really changes very little" [10]. The episode focused on forward strategy: Gordon revealed he was "doubling down on commercial" since the budget changes, predicting a coming rental boom with 11% to 47% rental growth in targeted markets [3][9]. He also used the New Zealand precedent — where negative gearing was removed in 2022 and reinstated in 2024 — to argue the changes might be temporary [5][8]. The message had evolved from criticism to opportunity: "these are the times of we're in a lull in the market right now" that sophisticated investors should exploit [7].

## Finding 4: Throughout June — Data-driven caution from the Suburb Data Podcast
The Suburb Data podcast (hosted by Damian and Jeremy) took a distinct approach, releasing market data roughly around the 6th of each month [1]. Their early-June episode analysed data running up to the end of May, showing days on market had increased approximately 6% across most capital cities — a noticeable post-budget shift — but they stressed that the market was "still very tight everywhere" with 34–39 days on market versus a normal expectation of around 60 days [3]. Vacancy rates remained extremely low (Darwin at 0.3–0.4%) [3][5]. Their stance was explicitly cautious and evidence-led: they expected the next one to two months of data to reveal the true market response to the "CGT and negative gearing changes" [2]. This channel did not take a political stance but instead served as a neutral barometer, confirming that while the budget had slowed activity, the fundamentals of supply shortage and population growth remained intact.

## Finding 5: The consistent strategic thread — hold grandfathered assets, pivot to commercial
A notable convergence across all channels was the strategic playbook they recommended. The KTG podcast insisted "we won't sell any of our properties which are grandfathered" and would instead "redirect as much of our hard savings... into paying down those debts first" on new post-budget assets [1][6]. The SPI/Investicate episode urged investors to "not stay paralyzed" and to follow a disciplined playbook based on long-term numbers [4]. Sammy Gordon confirmed the exit-and-consolidation strategy had not changed at all: "No man. No," when asked whether the budget altered his approach [7]. He further revealed that his firm had "been very aggressive... since budget changes" in the commercial property space, taking advantage of sellers cashing out [5]. This represented a cross-channel consensus: the budget changes were manageable for prepared investors, grandfathering created a powerful incentive to hold, and commercial property was emerging as the post-budget pivot of choice.

Across June 2026, the property channel’s stance on the budget’s tax changes evolved in two distinct phases, moving from an urgent, disruption-focused warning to a more measured clarification that downplayed the immediate impact.

**Phase 1 – June 10: Alarm over investor exodus, rent hikes, and a short window of opportunity**  
In the video *“The end of the old property playbook?”*, the channel argued that the removal of negative gearing would drive investors out of the market, shrink the rental supply, and force rents up by $100–$200 per week. Claims emphasised that the supply issues from the budget “haven't even come through yet” and that investors would stop buying existing residential, leading to a “massive shortage of rentals” ([g3], [g4], [g7], [g14]). The channel also warned that the “lower class will be decimated” by rent increases and that the “middle class are being shafted” ([g35], [g37]). At the same time, it framed the next six months as a “window of opportunity to buy well before rents increase” ([g11]), describing a “lull” that would precede a surge in rental growth ([g12], [g15], [g28]). The overall stance was that the changes were a major market disruptor requiring immediate attention.

**Phase 2 – June 15: Panic overblown, changes deferred, and misconceptions corrected**  
By June 15, in the follow-up video *“The budget has sparked panic, but has anything really changed yet?”*, the channel dramatically shifted tone. It now argued that “negative gearing is not gone despite misconceptions” and that properties bought before the budget (or even in June 2026) would still receive full benefits until July 2027 ([g46], [g47], [g48], [g51]). Crucially, the channel stressed that the cash-flow impact would not be felt until July 2028 at the earliest, and that “the biggest misconception is that no change from the budget will be felt until July 2028” ([g53], [g59]). It also noted that negative gearing deductions were deferred, not eliminated, and that CGT discounts still applied ([g55], [g56]). The stance became one of reassurance: the budget “has done a good job of confusing people” ([g54]) and the actual structural shift is years away, giving investors time to adjust.

**Summary of evolution**  
The channel’s stance moved from **early-June alarm** (imminent rental crisis, investor stampede, and a fleeting buying window) to **mid-June calm** (misinformation is rife, nothing material changes until mid-2028, and the panic is unwarranted). This shift reflects a deliberate effort to correct the initial, more dramatic narrative and provide a longer-term, more nuanced view of the policy’s timeline.

answers.answer: The agentic engineering workflow is presented as a five-part process [3], but the provided chunks elaborate mainly on the recruitment/onboarding phase and the post‑implementation validation pipeline. The high‑level steps are: 1) Assemble the ship (core setup), 2) Recruit and ramp up crew mates using memory files and skills, 3) Work with a single crew mate (planning + implementation + validation), 4) Work with multiple crew mates, 5) Recruit a first mate to manage overhead [3]. Within step 3, the workflow leverages a planning phase to clarify requirements with the agent, an autonomous implementation phase, and then a pipeline called “no mistakes” to review, test, document, and push changes [9][6][7]. The no mistakes pipeline leverages: branch creation, isolated worktree, intent analysis, rebasing, adversarial review, end‑to‑end testing with evidence recording, documentation updates, linting, and PR babysitting [6][7]. The onboarding step leverages global and project‑level memory files (with a symbolic link for agent compatibility) and skills (installed via a skill creator CLI) to teach agents how to work [8][10]. The workflow is designed to be agent agnostic and relies on terminal‑based efficiency [1][8], though the core specifics of steps 1, 4, and 5 are not detailed in the provided chunks.

The agentic engineering workflow described in the transcripts consists of several phases, each leveraging specific tools and principles:

1. **Assemble the ship (core setup)** – The user chooses a terminal‑based environment (e.g., Westerm) to keep the workflow keyboard‑only and reproducible across machines [5]. The setup is agent‑agnostic, meaning it works with any model or harness [8].
2. **Recruit and ramp up crew mates** – Fresh agent “recruits” are onboarded using **memory files** (global and project‑level) and **skills**. Memory files store preferences and project context; skills are extracted from memory for reusable tasks. The skill‑creator tool (from Anthropic, managed via Vercel’s CLI) teaches agents how to create skills [8][10].
3. **Work with a single crew mate** – The user clarifies requirements in a **planning phase**, then lets the agent implement autonomously. The user does not review diffs manually [9].
4. **Scale to multiple crew mates** – As complexity grows, the user works with several agents simultaneously [3].
5. **Recruit a first mate** – A first‑mate agent is introduced to manage overhead (e.g., coordination, routine tasks) so the user stays focused on high‑level decisions [3].
6. **No‑mistakes pipeline for quality** – After implementation, the change is sent through an automated pipeline called “no mistakes.” This pipeline:
   - Creates a branch, commits the change, and works in an isolated worktree [6].
   - Understands the user’s real intent by analyzing the agent session [6].
   - Rebases on the latest main branch and resolves merge conflicts upfront [6][7].
   - Runs an **adversarial review** (fresh context) that self‑corrects obvious problems and escalates ambiguous ones to the human [6][7].
   - Tests the change end‑to‑end against the original intent, recording evidence of correctness [7].
   - Updates documentation and ensures no linting problems before pushing the branch and raising a PR [7].
   - Babysits the PR until merge, handling merge conflicts and CI failures automatically [7].

The workflow leverages a **terminal‑first philosophy** [5], **agent‑agnostic tooling** [8], **memory files and skills** for onboarding [8], **thinking as an engineering manager/director** (not reviewing every diff) [6][9], and the **no‑mistakes pipeline** to automate quality assurance [6][7].

---

### 1. Memory File Setup and Organization

Global and project‑level memory files are organized as Markdown files that store agent preferences and project context. The **global memory file** (e.g., `agents.md`) is kept minimal (≈27 lines) and is symbolically linked into each agent's configuration so that every agent session loads the same core rules (e.g., never use m‑dash, avoid co‑author tags). It is stored in a central `files` repository and distributed via Home Manager, which creates symlinks to each agent's `CLAUDE.md` or equivalent location [s1.1][s1.4][s1.5].

**Project‑level memory files** (e.g., `CLAUD.md` or `agents.md`) are also maintained per project, again using symbolic links so multiple agents share the same file. These files are more verbose and contain project context, repository layout, terminology, end‑to‑end testing instructions, and collectively represent the learning from all agent sessions on that project. The file is built incrementally by correcting the agent and asking it to remember the fix, storing the lesson directly in the memory file. Over time, to reduce bloat, conditional information (e.g., testing instructions) is moved into separate **skills** that are loaded only when needed [s1.2][s1.3].

Synchronization is achieved via a rebuild script that reproduces the entire environment from the `files` repo on any machine, ensuring all agents consistently read the same global and project‑level memory files [s1.1].

---

### 2. First Mate Agent Capabilities

The **first mate** is a free, open‑source project that acts as a central coordinator. Setup is straightforward: clone the repository and run an agent inside it; the first interaction triggers a setup conversation where preferences (e.g., how strict to be, pipeline usage) are configured through natural dialogue [s2.3][s2.4].

Once active, the first mate handles overhead by:
- **Spinning up parallel tasks** – it creates new tmux tabs, uses the `treehouse` tool to create isolated worktrees, runs an agent in each worktree to complete the assigned work, and then triggers the **no‑mistakes pipeline** to validate the change and prepare a PR [s2.1].
- **Managing multiple projects simultaneously** – e.g., working on `lavish-axi`, `github-axi`, and `chrome-devtools-axi` at the same time by breaking one instruction into parallel tasks [s2.1].
- **Context switching** – the first mate juggles background agents, pulls open issues, discusses which ones are actionable, and assigns new tasks without the human needing to micromanage [s2.1][s2.2].
- **Freeing the human to act as a captain** – by taking over the constant coordination that would otherwise exhaust the user, the first mate allows the user to focus on big‑picture decisions like understanding user needs and setting direction [s2.2][s2.3].

Voice input is emphasized as a faster way to communicate with the first mate (e.g., using SuperWhisperer with custom system prompts for accurate transcription of project names) [s2.4]. The first mate can also leverage long‑running tools like **good night, have fun** for tasks that need to run overnight, but this tool is separate from the first mate itself [s2.5].

---

### 3. Adversarial Review Mechanism

The adversarial review is a step inside the **no‑mistakes pipeline**. The pipeline can be triggered as a skill by simply saying “no mistakes” to the agent, or it runs automatically when the first mate delegates work [s3.1][s3.3]. During the review:

- The pipeline creates a fresh agent context to review the change with “fresh eyes.” It self‑corrects obvious problems (e.g., code issues, missing documentation) and **fixes them before raising the PR** [s3.1].
- After self‑correction, the pipeline runs end‑to‑end tests and collects evidence (screenshots, video, log files) to demonstrate that the change meets the original intent [s3.1].
- The PR is then created with a summary of the original intent, what changed, how it was tested, and what the pipeline discovered and fixed. A **risk assessment** is included so the human can decide how much time to spend reviewing the diff. For low‑risk changes, the human trusts that the pipeline has already caught any issues; for high‑risk changes, the human conducts a more detailed review [s3.1][s3.2].

The provided chunks do not detail a formal escalation process for ambiguous problems. The first‑pass answer mentioned that ambiguous issues are escalated to the human, but the subtopic chunks only describe self‑correction and then human review of the PR. The escalation step may exist in the broader workflow but is not elaborated in the retrieved clips.

  "question": "Describe the Agentic Engineering Workflow: every step and what it leverages.",
  "answer": "## Key Findings\n1. The Agentic Engineering Workflow is structured as five escalating levels — from assembling a reproducible terminal environment to recruiting a First Mate that orchestrates all agents — enabling a single engineer to ship 40-50 well-tested PRs daily [1][4][6].\n2. Step 1 — \"Assembling the Ship\" — builds a fully reproducible development environment using Nix for declarative configuration, Wezterm as the terminal emulator, Tmux/Herder as the terminal multiplexer, and NeoVim as the editor, all managed from a single config repo [4][9][24].\n3. Step 2 — \"Recruit and Ramp Up Crew Mates\" — onboards agents via memory files (a minimal global memory file for cross-project preferences and a project-level memory file for accumulated learning) and skills (modular files using progressive disclosure to avoid token waste) [2][4][7].\n4. Step 3 — \"Working with a Single Crew Mate\" — uses voice input (3× faster than typing), interactive visual planning via Lavish AXI, hands-free autonomous implementation, and the No Mistakes pipeline (adversarial review, intent testing, documentation, PR babysitting) [1][5][11][12][13].\n5. Step 4 — \"Working with Multiple Crew Mates\" — leverages Good Night Have Fun for long-running iterative loops, Treehouse for zero-overhead git worktree management, and Herder/Tmux for managing parallel agent sessions [15][16][17][18].\n6. Step 5 — \"Recruit a First Mate\" — introduces an orchestrator agent that the human captain talks to, which automatically spins up worktrees, delegates tasks to agents, runs No Mistakes pipelines, and context-switches between projects [19][20][21].\n7. The entire workflow is agent-agnostic (works across Claude Code, Codex CLI, Pi, Open Code) and follows AXI design standards — 10 principles for building agent-ergonomic tools, e.g., token-efficient output formats saving ~40% versus JSON [2][3][10].\n\n## Finding 1: Assembling the Ship — Reproducible Terminal-Centric Foundation\n\nThe workflow begins by creating a fully reproducible development environment using Nix. The entire configuration — Wezterm (terminal emulator), Herder or Tmux (terminal multiplexer), NeoVim (editor), shell, fonts, and all packages — is managed declaratively. Kun uses Nix Darwin to configure macOS and Home Manager to distribute user-level packages, including a central global memory file that is symlinked into every agent harness's config location. Running a rebuild script on a freshly installed Mac clones the config repo and reproduces the exact same setup instantly [4][24][27]. The terminal-centric approach keeps the developer's hands on the keyboard and enables the exact same workflow even on a phone via SSH. Herder is highlighted as the recommended multiplexer because it was built for the agent era with native integration for agent harnesses like Claude Code and Codex CLI [9][25][26].\n\n## Finding 2: Recruiting and Ramping Up Crew Mates — Memory Files and Skills\n\nFresh agents have no context about the human's preferences or the project. Two mechanisms handle onboarding. Memory files come in two tiers: (1) a minimal global memory file (~27 lines) containing cross-project rules (e.g., \"never use em dash,\" \"don't add agent as co-author,\" \"when making technical decisions don't give too much weight to development cost\"), and (2) a verbose project-level memory file that accumulates collective learning from all agent sessions — when an agent makes a mistake, the human corrects it and stores the lesson [2][3][27]. Skills use progressive disclosure: on agent start, only a tiny description of each skill is loaded into the system prompt; when the agent decides it needs that skill, it reads the full file. This allows storing extensive conditional knowledge (e.g., end-to-end testing instructions) without inflating every request's token cost. Skills are managed via the `npx skills` CLI from Vercel, and the \"skill creator\" skill (by Anthropic) teaches agents to create new skills themselves [4][7]. A strong warning is given against installing unverified skills — even popular repos with 177k stars have been shown to degrade performance [7].\n\n## Finding 3: Working with a Single Crew Mate — Voice, Lavish Planning, and No Mistakes\n\nInteraction starts with voice input via Open Super Whisper (local, open-source speech recognition), which a Stanford paper showed is 3× faster than typing. For complex features, the agent uses Lavish AXI — an interactive HTML-based planning tool that renders options as a visual artifact matching the project's design system, replacing the traditional wall of text. The human can annotate, click decisions, and give feedback directly in the browser, making requirement refinement dramatically more efficient [1][5][11]. Once planning is done, the human says \"start building\" and leaves the agent to implement autonomously. When the agent reports completion, the change is sent into the No Mistakes pipeline, which: creates an isolated git worktree, understands the real intent from the agent session, rebases on latest main, runs an adversarial review in a fresh context window (self-correcting obvious problems, escalating ambiguous ones), tests the change end-to-end with recorded evidence, updates documentation, checks linting, pushes a PR, and babysits the PR until merge handling CI failures and new conflicts [12][13][14]. The human only reviews the risk assessment on the PR — for low-risk changes, the diff is not inspected at all [6][14].\n\n## Finding 4: Working with Multiple Crew Mates — Parallelism at Scale\n\nTo keep multiple agents working simultaneously, three tools are layered. Good Night Have Fun is a long-running loop tool for objectives like \"find every usability problem as a 7-year-old\" — it iterates autonomously until a stop condition, making commits that the human can review later. Running parallel agents in the same repo causes conflicts, solved by git worktrees — separate directories on the filesystem. However, manually managing worktrees creates mental overhead. Treehouse automates this: running `treehouse` drops the human into a fresh worktree, `treehouse status` lists all worktrees and their usage, and closing the tab automatically frees the worktree for future reuse [15][16][17][18]. With Herder's agent-aware multiplexing, the human can run multiple agent sessions in parallel tabs, switch between them via keyboard shortcuts, and monitor real-time status (model, context usage) from a side panel — without needing to context-switch into each session manually [5][18].\n\n## Finding 5: The First Mate — From Sailor to Captain\n\nManaging multiple parallel agent sessions eventually becomes exhausting due to constant context-switching. The final escalation inserts a First Mate, an open-source orchestrator agent that the human talks to as captain. The human says \"work on these three GitHub projects and add an update command to each,\" and the First Mate decomposes this into parallel tasks, spins up Tmux tabs, calls Treehouse to create worktrees, runs agents in each worktree, triggers No Mistakes pipelines, and context-switches between projects automatically [19][20][21]. This shifts the bottleneck from task execution to idea generation — the captain starts running out of ideas of what to ask, which signals the need to focus outward on users, competition, and strategic direction. The ultimate outcome is a successful transition from \"sailor\" (doing the work) to \"captain\" (setting the treasure map) [21][22].\n\n## Finding 6: AXI Design Standards — Agent-Ergonomic Tooling\n\nUnderpinning the entire workflow is AXI — a set of 10 design principles Kun authored for building tools that treat agents as first-class citizens, optimizing for \"agent ergonomics.\" For example, using token-efficient output formats saves ~40% tokens compared to JSON, and reducing unnecessary turns and latency improves both cost and success rate. Concrete implementations include GitHub AXI (benchmarked to have the lowest cost and highest success rate versus the GitHub MCP server or CLI), Chrome DevTools AXI, and Lavish AXI. The catalog is available at axi.md, and the entire workflow is deliberately agent-agnostic — it works with Claude Code, Codex CLI, Pi, Open Code, or any other harness because the landscape changes rapidly [2][3][10].",

answers.answer:
The **Agentic Engineering Workflow** unfolds in five stages, moving from foundation to autonomous scaling. Each stage leverages specific tools and patterns to keep the human in a “captain” role while agents handle execution.

1. **Assembling the ship (core setup)**  
   The foundation is a **keyboard‑driven terminal** (the emulator *Westerm*). Working entirely in the terminal forces hands‑on‑keyboard discipline and makes the exact same workflow reproducible on any device, even a phone [5]. The harness (e.g. Claude Code) is chosen to be **agent‑agnostic** so that the workflow survives rapid model turnover [8].

2. **Recruiting & ramping up crew mates (memory + skills)**  
   Fresh agents know nothing about the project. They are onboarded with **memory files** – a global file (`agents.md`) and project‑level files – linked together via a symbolic link so every agent reads the same rules [8]. Conditionally useful instructions are extracted from memory into **skills**, which agents can create on their own after installing a `skill‑creator` skill [10]. This shift keeps memory files lean and token‑efficient.

3. **Working with a single crew mate (plan‑then‑build)**  
   The session splits into two phases: **planning** (clarifying requirements) and **implementation** (agent writes code). The human stays hands‑off during implementation, only returning when the agent signals “done” [9].

4. **When the agent says done – the *no mistakes* pipeline**  
   Instead of manually reviewing diffs (which bottlenecks throughput), the work is handed to a **free, open‑source pipeline called *no mistakes*** [6]. It orchestrates the change through:  
   - Creating a branch and commit in an isolated work tree.  
   - Understanding the real intent from the agent session.  
   - Rebasing on the latest remote `main` and resolving merge conflicts.  
   - Running an **adversarial review** in a fresh context – obvious problems self‑correct; ambiguous issues are escalated to the human.  
   - Testing the change end‑to‑end against intent, recording evidence of correctness.  
   - Updating all relevant documentation.  
   - Running a lint pass, pushing the branch, and raising a PR.  
   - **Babysitting** the PR until merge – handling merge conflicts and CI failures automatically [6][7].  

   This frees the human from diff‑reviewing drudgery and removes the reviewer‑bottleneck.

5. **Multi‑agent coordination & a first mate**  
   After mastering a single agent, the workflow scales to **multiple crew mates working simultaneously**. Finally, a **first mate** (a meta‑agent) is recruited to handle operational overhead, letting the human captain remain focused on the big picture [3].

In summary, the workflow leverages: a pure‑terminal environment for portability; symbolic‑linked memory files and extractable skills for agent ramp‑up; a plan‑then‑implement session pattern for clarity; the *no mistakes* pipeline to automate review, testing, and PR management; and agent‑agnostic tooling to stay adaptable.

The best-practice resume structure is a concise, keyword‑optimised sales pitch aimed at passing ATS filters and grabbing a recruiter’s attention in 6–8 seconds ([9], [6]). The core sections are:

1. **Header** – your name, role title (e.g., “Data Engineer” – not “aspiring” or “enthusiast”), LinkedIn, GitHub, and location. No photo, graphics, or tagline ([3], [6]).
2. **Skills / Tech Stack** – group relevant skills logically. A separate skills section helps ATS parsers catch keywords without having to scan the whole experience section ([6]).
3. **Professional Summary** – a short statement (3–4 paragraphs or a few lines) that tells hiring managers how long you have been doing the work and what you are best at, ideally backed with facts and figures ([g29], [4], [10]). Use a plug‑and‑play template to structure it ([g30], [10]).
4. **Experience** – the “moat” of your resume ([3]). List jobs from most recent to least recent ([7], [22]). For each role, write **action‑oriented accomplishment bullet points** that prove impact (e.g., quantified results, projects you architected or led) rather than generic responsibilities ([8], [2], [3], [7]).
5. **Projects** – critical for freshers or entry‑level professionals; less important for senior hires ([3]).
6. **Education & Certifications** – mention your degree (no GPA unless impressive) and third‑party certifications (AWS, Databricks, etc.). Skip Udemy certificates ([3]). For experienced hires, education goes at the bottom ([5]).

**What to delete entirely**: objective statements, hobbies, references, “references available on request,” photos, and generic buzzwords ([g14], [3], [6]).

**Types of experiences to include**: focus on **relevant, recent work** that aligns with the target job. Shuffle or summarise old roles that are no longer applicable ([2]). For each bullet point, demonstrate **clear ownership**—explain what you architected, designed, led, and the platforms/technologies used ([2], [25]). Use a formula: *action verb + what you did + measurable result* ([8], [3]). If you have long experience (8+ years), remove or condense very old positions ([5]).

Keep the entire resume to one page if possible; two pages is acceptable for experienced professionals, but avoid listing every achievement ([2], [7]). Include a link to your LinkedIn profile—resumes with a LinkedIn URL have a 71% better chance of hearing back ([g6]).

conversations.question: tell me how should I structure my resume profressional summary give me how many lines and the topic I cover for each line in the summary

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
## Key Findings

1. Aim for a professional summary of about 2–3 lines (2–3 sentences), though one expert says 1–2 sentences max and others trim it to roughly two tight sentences [1][6][7][8].
2. Line/sentence 1 should answer "Who are you?" — your professional title/role, level, years of experience, and the environments/industries you've worked in [4][9][10].
3. Line/sentence 2 should answer "What can you do?" — the parts of the work you're best at and your top relevant skills [2][10].
4. Line/sentence 3 (or woven into line 2) should answer "Are you any good?" — proof via specific, quantified accomplishments and impact with facts and figures [2][3][4][9].
5. Write the summary last (after the rest of the resume) so it acts as a thesis the rest of the resume proves, and tailor it per application rather than using boilerplate [6][7][8].

## Finding 1: Length — keep it to 2–3 lines
The consistent guidance across the transcripts is to keep the professional summary short. One reviewer suggests reducing a summary to "just two to three lines" to free up space for work experience [1], another recommends "one to two sentences max" [8], and a third suggests a "two to three sentence professional summary" that he then tightens to "about two sentences" to make it "lean and useful" [6][7]. The reason for the brevity: hiring managers spend only about six seconds scanning a resume, so the summary must win them over instantly [2].

## Finding 2: Line 1 — Who you are (role, years, environments)
The first line should establish your identity: "what we are, marketing leader or whatever it is, years experience, environments in which we have done our work" [4]. In practice this means your core function, your level, and your industry — e.g., "e-commerce expert" that covers "what we do, the level we're at, and the industry that we're in" [10]. Another expert frames it as: tell them "exactly how long we've been doing work like this" and "the parts of the work that we are best at" [2]. You can also skip re-listing tech stacks here if they're already obvious from your experience section, to save space [1].

## Finding 3: Line 2 — What you can do (top skills and expertise)
The second line covers your strongest, job-relevant skills and areas of expertise, making the reader "feel confident in our skills and our ability to do the job well" [2]. The overall summary should answer the three questions — "Who are you? What can you do? and are you any good?" — where "what you can do" is demonstrated by listing your top skills, ideally pulled from the job postings you're applying to [10]. This line should be specific and relevant to the role (e.g., matching the exact tech stack the recruiter is hiring for) so the reader can save time instead of reading the whole resume [8].

## Finding 4: Line 3 — Proof: accomplishments with facts and figures
By the second or third line you should stop telling and start proving: "by the second sentence, you should be bragging about specific accomplishments that you've achieved" [4]. Use "facts and figures based on accomplishments we achieved in previous roles" so the reader thinks "wow, you did that for your last employer — I want to hire you" [3]. The template advice is to "double down on what job we've been doing," share years of experience, and then "share some examples of extremely impressive accomplishments" with numbers and specifics [9][11]. Avoid generic "passionate programmer" fluff — the summary's whole point is specific, relevant information [8].

## Finding 5: Adapt the structure to your situation, and write it last
The same 2–3 line skeleton adapts to your career stage: career changers use a line to show they are "eagerly learning" the new discipline, new professionals showcase "potential and the effort we're willing to put forward to learn and grow," and the strongest version blends "experience, skills, relationship building and impact" plus character [3][5][11]. Two process rules recur: write the summary after the rest of the resume is done so it "truly summarizes" and acts like "a thesis that the rest of your resume must prove" [6][7], and don't use a boilerplate summary that isn't changed per application [8].

conversations.question: for a resume how should I set up the techincal skill section

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
Based on my research across the transcript corpus, here is the synthesized answer.

## Key Findings
1. The technical skills section should be a plain list of programming languages, platforms, and tools — no rating bars, sparklines, or charts [1].
2. The list must be tailored to the specific job description, with keywords pulled from target postings (often with AI help) [11][2][8][15].
3. Placement matters: skills go right after the summary and before experience for most roles, near the top for specialized roles, and at the bottom for experienced hires [7][13][10].
4. Specialize rather than dumping every skill — hiring managers want specialists, not generalists [12][13][14].
5. Avoid redundancy and generic filler: don't repeat the same skills across sections, and skip generic traits like "attention to detail" [5][18][2].
6. A bare skill list isn't enough — tie the skills into your experience bullet points so they're evidenced [15][12][19].

## Finding 1: Keep it simple — no charts or ratings
The core advice is to simply list the names of programming languages, platforms, tools, and general skills that match the job description you're applying for [1]. Fancy bar charts, sparklines, or elaborate rating systems are explicitly discouraged — "Your resume isn't a Yelp review" [1]. The skills list should be quick to scan since recruiters spend only 6–8 seconds on a resume after ATS filtering [17].

## Finding 2: Tailor the list to the job description
The recommended workflow is to read job descriptions for hard technical skills, soft skills, and product qualities ("-ilities") [11]. You can paste 2–3 target job descriptions into an AI engine with a prompt asking for a prioritized list of hard skills, technology, job functions, and industry terminology, explicitly avoiding generic entry-level skills [2][8]. Similar keyword-extraction approaches (word clouds, AI prompts producing ~25 one-to-three-word keywords) are used to populate the skills section [8][15]. Skills should match the tasks, software, and terminology mentioned in the postings [3].

## Finding 3: Placement and ordering
The skills section normally goes right after the professional summary and definitely before the experience section [7]. For specialized roles, having skills near the top makes it easy for a hiring manager to confirm you're proficient in exactly what they need [13]. For experienced hires, however, the skills section (and projects/education) belongs at the bottom, since experience is the "moat" [10]. For students and new grads, education goes above skills [6]. The section should not be buried on page two, and shouldn't take up excessive vertical space [7].

## Finding 4: Specialize, don't list everything
Hiring managers notice whether you "list every single skill under the sun or are you specialized" [12]. If someone is hiring a frontend engineer, they want a skill set revolving around the specific stack (e.g., Next.js and MUI), not every UI library [13]. "Nobody likes hiring a generalist. Everyone likes hiring a specialist" [13], and specializing in too many things waters your application down [14]. Listing a skill like React without work experience to back it up is also weak — reviewers look for whether you use it daily at a job [12].

## Finding 5: Avoid redundancy and generic filler
A common mistake is having both a general skills section and a separate technical skills section that repeat the same items — that redundancy should be removed [5]. Generic, repetitive skills should also be dropped: avoid listing both "leadership" and "team leadership," and skip vague entry-level traits like "attention to detail" and "teamwork" [18][2]. Some reviewers even argue the skills section can be removed entirely if your skills are already obvious from your work experience and projects [4][5].

## Finding 6: Back the skills up with evidence
Adding keywords to a skills section alone is not enough — hiring managers need proof you have them [15]. The recommended approach is to weave those keywords into experience bullet points, e.g., with bolded skill titles at the start of each bullet, tying the listed skills to the keywords pulled from the job description [15][8]. Mirroring the job posting's verbiage in your bullets makes you sound like someone already in the role [19]. A separate skills section does help ATS parse your skills without combing the whole experience section, so it has scanning value if kept [9].

## Finding 7: Formatting for ATS and readability
Use standard section headings like "Skills" so ATS can categorize information correctly, and use the right keywords throughout [8]. Group skills logically [9]. A compact design trick is to use a borderless table (e.g., 3x4) with bullets to save vertical space, and drop body text (including the skills section) to a 10-point font for a condensed, professional look [7][16].

answers.answer: Keep the technical skills section simple and plain: list the names of programming languages, platforms, tools, and general skills that match the job description, without bar charts, sparklines, or rating systems [1]. Use concrete tools rather than broad subject labels—for example, write Python with numpy/pandas, deployment with Flask/FastAPI, and cloud with AWS EC2/S3 instead of just “machine learning” or “statistics” [3]. Pull hard skills, technology/equipment, job functions, and industry terminology from target job descriptions to decide what to include [2]. Place the skills section before the experience section, usually after the professional summary, and keep it visually compact (e.g., a borderless table with bullets) rather than letting it sprawl over a page [9]. Avoid redundancy: if a separate “technical skills” subsection repeats skills already in your skills list, remove it [5].

Set up your technical skills section as a **short, scannable, keyword-rich list near the top of your resume** — not a flashy design or a generic laundry list — and make sure every skill is backed up somewhere else in the resume.

- **Placement:** Put the skills section high on the page. One approach is to place it directly at the top and even replace the summary section [g7]; another is to put it right after your professional summary and before experience [9]. If you are a student or recent grad, education can go above skills [4].
- **Content:** List actual tools, languages, platforms, and frameworks — not broad subjects. For example, write “Python with NumPy/pandas/scikit-learn, deployment with Flask/FastAPI, cloud with AWS EC2/S3” instead of “machine learning / statistics” [3]. Don’t list obvious things like using Mac OS or Windows [g2].
- **Tailor to the job:** Pull the key skills from job descriptions you’re targeting, because recruiters and resume scanners look for specific keywords from a predefined list [g19][g21][2]. Avoid generic filler such as “attention to detail and teamwork” unless truly relevant [2].
- **Design:** Don’t use bar charts, sparklines, or rating systems — just list the names of languages, platforms, tools, and general skills [1]. Keep it compact; one effective option is a simple borderless table with bullets [9]. Use bold sparingly for important keywords [g14].
- **Avoid redundancy:** If your experience already makes your technical skills obvious, don’t add a separate technical-skills section that just repeats them [5].
- **Show proof:** Skills listings alone don’t convince — briefly demonstrate your abilities through experience and projects [g9][g18]. Frame skills as applied tools, not course subjects, so recruiters see real work rather than theory [3].

answers.answer: To set up the technical-skill section, list plain names of programming languages, platforms, tools, and job-relevant skills — no bar charts, sparklines, ratings, or elaborate designs [1]. Write specific technologies rather than broad subjects: for example, list "Python with numpy/pandas/PyTorch, deployment with Flask/FastAPI, cloud with AWS EC2/S3" instead of just "machine learning" [3]. Group skills logically, and consider keeping a separate skills/tech-stack section so an ATS doesn't have to parse your whole experience section for keywords [10]. Place the skills section before experience and format it compactly — for instance, using a borderless table with bullet points — to avoid awkward white space [8]. Avoid creating a redundant "technical skill" section that repeats your main skills; if your skills are already obvious from your work experience, you can remove the section to save space [5]. Note that the sources differ slightly: one recommends a dedicated grouped skills section for ATS matching [10], while another advises removing it if it duplicates what experience already shows [5].

answers.answer: Keep it simple: list your technical and soft skills as plain names of programming languages, platforms, tools, and general skills that match the job description, without bar charts, sparklines, or rating systems [1][8]. Place the skills section before the experience section (typically after the professional summary) [7], though experienced hires may want it near the bottom since the experience section is what matters most [10]. Avoid redundancy—if you already have a skills section, don't repeat the same items in a separate "Technical Skills" section, and consider removing the skill section entirely if your skills are obvious from your work experience [4]. Finally, recruiters generally look for qualifications demonstrated in experience rather than just keywords in a skills section, so back up each listed skill with concrete impact in your experience bullets [9].

The recommended formula is exactly: action verb plus specific tech plus measurable impact — e.g., \"built a Spark-based ETL pipeline processing 2 TB of daily event data, reducing downstream query latency by 60%\" [7]. A weak bullet (\"built a customer support chatbot using OpenAI API\") becomes delivery evidence when rewritten as \"designed and deployed a RAG-based support assistant (LangChain + OpenAI + FastAPI) that auto-resolved 70% of tier-1 tickets, cutting average response time from 4 hours to 90 seconds.\" The bad versions describe activity; the good versions describe what you did, the tech stack, and the needle that moved [7].\n\n## Finding 2: Frame each app as a client delivery with a measurable business outcome\nThe experience section should be about one thing: impact — how you used your skills to make money, save money, save time, or increase productivity for your organization or your customers [10]. For consultancy-style work, recruiters explicitly want the how, the reason, and the result — the \"how and why + result\" matters more than the \"what\" [14]. Since personal projects without real users count for less than production-ready code with real users [15], your \"AI Engineer — Independent\" framing is exactly right: it turns each app into a delivered engagement with a stakeholder outcome. Use the Resume Formula — \"I accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z\" — on every line [9]. Example structure per app: problem/scoped need → solution built → measured result.\n\n## Finding 3: Keep it tight — 2–3 bullets max per entry, in \"I did X using Y\" format\nResume reviewers consistently recommend limiting bullet points to a maximum of 2–3 per role, written as \"I did X using Y,\" with metrics attached where credible [8]. Zen (ex-GitHub engineer) specifically calls out long, bullet-heavy experience sections as a waste of space and recommends capping entries at three bullets for consistency [6]. So for each app you list under the role, give it at most 1–2 formula bullets — one strong \"delivery\" bullet plus optionally one \"scale/outcome\" bullet — rather than a laundry list of tasks.\n\n## Finding 4: Lead with your North Star app so the AI skills are self-evident\nPut your top project, your North Star project, at the very top of the section so skills like building scalable AI solutions are obvious from the project description alone — \"show, not tell\" [1]. A keystone AI project plus a resume story that builds toward AI engineering is more important than nitpicking individual bullet points [5]. For an independent consultant, a real project delivered to clients is real work and gives you a concrete, credible bridge into AI engineering roles [4]. Order your apps from strongest to least impressive.\n\n## Finding 5: Hyperlink every app to GitHub or a live demo to prove it is real\nResumes with projects but no way to check their validity get flagged — embedded links to GitHub pages or live apps cost no extra space and let people verify the work is real [2][3]. Conversely, links that are broken, outdated, or point to a dead deployment actively hurt you, so only include links that work and look good [8].\n\n## Finding 6: Add a tech-stack line under each app with AI-engineer keywords\nAfter each work experience entry, include the relevant technologies and keywords you worked with [12]. For AI engineer roles specifically, recruiters screen for AI, LLM, NLP, Python (preferred), agentic frameworks (LangChain, Crew, MCP, A2A), generative AI such as RAG, ML frameworks like TensorFlow/PyTorch, API design, cloud, and CI/CD — and these \"cannot be in a skill section,\" they need to show up as qualifications in your experience [13]. conversations.question: on a resume what is the best approach for writing up previous job experiences is it company / role / tech stack and a couple of dot points for key skills demonstrated

## Key Findings

1. The standard experience-entry format is company + job title + dates (+ location), most recent job first, with the title bolded and full months (not just years) listed [1][2].
2. Bullet points should be accomplishment statements, not generic duties — the widely recommended formula is "Action verb + specific tech + measurable impact" [3][4].
3. Your bullets should prove business impact (made money, saved money, saved time, or increased efficiency), not restate your old job description [5][6].
4. Listing a tech stack per role is good practice: include the relevant technologies/keywords after each work experience, and weave them into bullets so ATS systems and hiring engineers can see what you used day-to-day [8][9].
5. Keep it tight — roughly 2–3 bullets per job, with numbers/metrics where honest, varied action verbs, and keywords pulled from the job description [12][13][11].

## Finding 1: The standard entry format: company, role, dates, location
The consensus format for each job entry is the company on the left with the dates on the right, the job title below the company, and then the bullet points [2]. Your job title should be bolded (it's what readers care about most), the location in italics to differentiate it from the company, and you should include the actual months you were in the role rather than just years — "2023 to 2024" hides whether that was two weeks or two years [1]. Entries must go from most recent job back to least recent, with no exceptions, because ATS scanners read in that order and it's how people naturally scan [1].

## Finding 2: Bullets should be accomplishments, not responsibilities
Your "couple of dot points" should not just describe what you were responsible for or demonstrate that you have skills — hiring managers don't care about activities, they care about impact [3]. The recommended formula is "Action verb + specific tech + measurable impact," e.g., "Built a Spark-based ETL pipeline processing 2 TB of daily event data, reducing query latency by 60%" rather than "Used SQL and PySpark for data analysis" [3]. Similarly, "action-oriented accomplishment bullet points" prove you were great at the work, whereas bullets that just describe generic responsibilities get no interviews [4]. Your experience section is explicitly *not* the place for your previous job descriptions — it's about impact only [5].

## Finding 3: Use an impact formula tied to business outcomes
A simple, effective structure for each bullet is the Resume Formula: "I accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z" [6]. When reviewing your work history, look for direct impact related to making money, saving money, saving time, or driving efficiency; when you can't tie to those, look for indirect impact — anything that led to a positive result [7]. One source also notes that every bullet should translate your past work into the reader's business priorities, mirroring the job description's language so you sound like someone who drives outcomes [13-cite? — I'll use the eGmZZFJ-8PY chunk]. Actually let me be careful: I have evidence from eGmZZFJ-8PY (04:18-05:32) about translating into business priorities. I'll include that.

## Finding 4: Tech stack placement — list it per role and inside bullets
Yes, include the tech stack per job: one advisor's tip is to list your role and location, write bullet points quantifying your contributions, and then "after each work experience include the relevant Technologies and keywords that you have worked with" [8]. Another resume reviewer says mentioning the technologies you used in the bullets is great because engineers want to know whether you use them day-to-day or just occasionally [9]. A separate skills/tech-stack section also helps because ATS systems can parse it without having to work through the whole experience section [10]. The big risk to avoid is a tech stack that mismatches the job description — a resume listing AWS/Snowflake/Airflow can get thrown out if the job wants Azure/ADF/Looker [4-in-2nd-call? I'll use 3pFRqPqzBCM 06:53-07:59 — that's the tech stack mismatch mistake].

## Finding 5: Keep it tight: 2–3 bullets, honest numbers, keyword-tied
You generally want at most two to three bullet points per job, in the shape of "I did X using Y," with metrics attached if you have them [12]. Numbers help ("the more the better"), every bullet should start with a strong action verb, and you should vary your wording so it doesn't read like AI-generated copy [13]. One caution: fabricating precise metrics (e.g., "lowered error rates by 87.3%") is viewed skeptically by reviewers, so only attach numbers you can stand behind [9]. Finally, to make "skills demonstrated" actually land, add bolded mini-titles at the start of your bullets that tie each bullet to keywords pulled from the job description — that gets past ATS and impresses human readers [11].

conversations.question: Review my portfolio site https://nmp-dsci.github.io/ against what the corpus says about presenting engineering work to hiring managers — what should I change?

answers.title: rag_llm (single-hop)
answers.answer:
Here is the review of the page text I was given; the About page linked in [§1] and the case-study targets behind [§3], [§4], [§5], [§6], [§7], and [§8] were not fetched.

1. Put code links on the project cards. The GitHub link appears in [§1] and again in the footer after [§9], but the cards [§3], [§4], [§5], [§6], [§7], and [§8] each end with "Case study →" and no repo link is visible in the card text. The corpus says projects should have embedded links to GitHub so reviewers can check that they are real [7]. Add a "Repo →" or "Code →" link to every card; if a project is closed-source, follow [1] and show a demo/dummy dashboard instead.

2. Add a scannable skills/keyword block. The hero [§2] names "agentic systems, RAG pipelines and the eval harnesses", and technologies like "AWS App Runner" [§4] and "optimiser-tuned prompts" [§6] are buried in project copy. No section labelled "Skills" appears in the text I inspected. The corpus says to put skills first with all AI engineering technologies highlighted [4], and to treat keywords as a top priority [3]. Add a compact stack line under [§2] — e.g., "Agents · RAG · evals · guardrails · AWS" — so a skimming recruiter sees the keywords immediately.

3. Add the "why" behind architectural choices. The corpus says a project explanation should be a series of decisions and trade-offs — "Why this database over another one? Why this API design?" [8]. [§3] states "a deterministic policy gate between the model and every action" but not why that pattern is the right one; [§4] says "governed SQL out" but not why you chose that over another access pattern. Add one trade-off line to each card, especially [§3], [§4], and [§6].

conversations.question: How should I prepare for behavioural interview questions?

answers.title: rag_llm (single-hop)
answers.answer: Build a reusable "story bank" of five or six stories and answer behavioural questions using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) [2]. Practice the stories out loud, ideally in front of a mirror or camera, and do it consistently so you do not blank during the interview [1][2]. You can use a Notion behavioural template with common questions and a work summary, and use an agent/AI to update outdated answers before polishing them [1][4]. Keep a running doc of the interview questions you were actually asked and the answers you gave so your bank grows over time [5]. Before every interview, predict likely questions and plan answers in advance [3]. Also remember that stories that feel too small are still worth telling, because interviewers have never heard them [1][5]. Finally, prepare good questions to ask the interviewer at the end, such as what a successful new hire looks like [5].
contexts: questions that a lot of companies will ask. My problem is all my answers for these questions are very outdated. They're from an older story bank. So, all I'm going to do is ask Notion to update the answers in the behavioral questions table using the content that's been saved in my work summary. And this will help me generate new story bank that I can use to practice my behavioral interview questions with. I really like to get in front of a mirror and then answer all these questions like talking to myself or talking to a camera just so that I'm prepared to recite like these stories. And what's cool is my custom agent can be updated on a trigger. Every time I update my work summary, I can add new story bank answers. So, I'm going to take a look at the answers it generated, polish them up, and then I'll be done my behavioral section. So, when I was first preparing for behavioral interviews, I really struggled because I didn't know what stories were worth telling. I kept thinking, is this even impressive enough to bring up? I would think of something I did at school or a previous internship and immediately talk myself out of it because it felt too small or obvious.

get better. Just do it consistently and practice your questions out loud. Imagine getting to this point of the interview and then you just blank on your interview stories because you didn't have any prepared. In my Amazon interview, I think I talked to the person 20 minutes over my interview time because I was just like so excited to talk and I like loved yapping. So, I think I'm actually like not too bad at the behavioral part. Amazon has these 16 core values called leadership principles. conversations.question: What are the key tax changes affecting property investors right now?

answers.title: rag_llm (summary-filtered)
answers.answer: The budget proposed four key tax changes affecting property investors [8]. First, negative gearing: properties held before budget night (12 May, 7:30pm) retain existing negative-gearing benefits; going forward it applies only until 1 July 2027 for all properties and only to new properties after that [8]. For buyers of existing properties, losses are quarantined and carried forward rather than refunded [4]. Second, CGT: a new indexation method is being reintroduced (removed in 1999) [7]; most properties would need a market valuation with a 50% CGT calculation up to the 1 July 2027 market value, followed by indexation, plus a proposed minimum 30% tax rate on real capital gains [6]. Third, trusts: trustees would face a 30% flat tax on distributions, and distributions to corporate beneficiaries/bucket companies could trigger extra tax/double taxation [6]. Fourth, WATTO (Working Australian's Tax Offset) was named but not explained in the transcript [8]. Grandfathered investors appear likely to hold existing properties [1][5], SMSFs were not touched [9], and the speakers say the changes haven't altered supply/demand fundamentals, though they may reduce rentals in established areas [1][2]. These are proposed measures subject to legislation and possible changes in government [4].

conversations.question: How do I make my resume ATS-friendly?

answers.title: rag_llm (single-hop)
answers.answer: To make your resume ATS-friendly, use a clean, simple one-column template and avoid graphics, photos, tables, headers/footers, colors, emojis, symbols, and columns, since these can confuse ATS parsing [3][5][7]. Save it as a PDF rather than a Word or Google doc, keep margins consistent (1 inch, or 0.5 inch if needed), use standard section headings like "Experience" and "Skills", and use an easy-to-read font such as Arial or Times New Roman at 11–12 pt [3][4][7][8]. Because ATS software screens resumes automatically [6], you should keyword optimize by pulling important terms from the job description (for example, by asking an AI for the 25 most important keywords) and weaving them into your summary and bullet points [1][2][9]. Hiring managers also scan for relevant keywords, so including too much irrelevant information hurts your chances [10]. On length, the retrieved chunks conflict: some say one page [4][10], while another says 1–1.5 pages for entry/mid-level and 2–2.5 pages for those with 8+ years of experience [5].

answers.answer: To make your resume ATS-friendly, use a simple, clean layout: avoid graphics, colors, tables, footers, headers, images, emojis, columns, and symbols, because ATS can struggle with complex designs and may misread columns or skip content [3][7]. Keep your resume to one page if possible, use consistent margins (1 inch, or reduce to 0.5 inch if needed), stick to basic fonts like Arial or Times New Roman at 11–12pt, save it as a PDF, and use standard section headings like Experience or Skills [3][4][8]. Crucially, keyword optimize your resume: upload your resume and the job description to an AI tool, ask for a list of the 25 most important keywords for the job, then weave those keywords into your skills section and bullet points [2][10]. You can also start with a clean ATS-optimized template [1][9].

conversations.question: What should the professional summary at the top of a resume say?

answers.title: rag_llm (single-hop)
answers.answer: The professional summary should be a short pitch that identifies you and sells the reader on you quickly, since hiring managers may spend only seconds deciding whether to keep or discard the resume [3]. It should open with who you are (e.g., title, level, years of experience, industry/environments), then in the second sentence pivot to bragging about specific, impressive accomplishments and facts/figures that prove you are good at the work [1], [3], [4]. Keep it to about two sentences or two to three lines, phrased like a thesis the rest of the resume has to prove, and write it after the rest of the resume is done [7], [9], [10]. Tailor the emphasis to your situation: experienced professionals should stress tenure and strengths, career changers should show eager, active learning of the new field, and new professionals should show potential and willingness to grow [2], [6]. Above all, don't just restate a job title or duties—make it accomplishment-oriented [1], [2], [4].

answers.answer: At the top of a resume, the professional summary should be a brief, roughly two-sentence “thesis” that tells the reader who you are and why they should hire you, rather than merely stating that you want a job [2][3][5]. It should open with what you are, your years of experience, and the environments/industries you have worked in, then—by the second sentence—brag about specific accomplishments, ideally with facts, figures, and numbers [3][2][9]. This helps the reader think, “wow, you did that for your last employer—I want you to do that for me” [2]. If you are changing careers or are a new professional, the summary should instead emphasize your potential, eagerness, and effort to learn the new field [1]. Write it last, keep it tight and free of fluff, and make sure every claim is backed up in your experience section [5][7][10]. The chunks mention plug-and-play templates, but the transcripts do not include the actual template wording, so I can only describe the components, not quote the full template [4][9].

conversations.question: How should I write my LinkedIn about section and skills so recruiters find me?

answers.title: rag_llm (single-hop)
answers.answer: Start your about section with keywords: review 5–10 job descriptions, paste them into a word cloud generator, and use the most frequent terms in 3–4 concise paragraphs that introduce your experience, highlight skills and impact with numbers, and state the types of opportunities you want [1]. Put those same keywords in your about, experience, and skill sections, because recruiters search LinkedIn using those terms [5]. For the skills section, pick five skills from the word cloud based on the job you want, add them to your profile, and ask colleagues, friends, family, or classmates to endorse them—LinkedIn only counts skills with at least one endorsement, and you need five such skills to fully use the section [2]. Alternatively, paste 2–3 target job descriptions into an AI tool and prompt it to list hard skills, technology, job functions, industry terminology, and leadership skills while avoiding generic terms like attention to detail [3]. You can add up to 100 skills, but avoid repetitive ones like "leadership" and "team leadership" [3][9].

conversations.question: What does a recruiter actually look for on an AI engineer resume?

answers.title: rag_llm (single-hop)
answers.answer: Recruiters first check high-level logistics and surface fit: location, updated contact info, technologies matching the job description, willingness to work in office, and visa eligibility — and since they aren't always technical, they may pass your resume to an engineer to confirm the technical claims [1]. For an AI-engineer role specifically, a recruiter's checklist is fairly concrete: AI, LLM, NLP, Python (preferred over C/Java), agile/architecture design of AI, agentic tools like Langchain, Crew, MCP and A2A, generative AI such as RAG, ML frameworks like TensorFlow/PyTorch, Git/GitHub API design, cloud, NumPy, R/Matlab, SDLC/CI/CD/DevOps, and explaining tech to non-technical people, with SDKs as a nice-to-have; candidates need about 75% of those and cannot just paste them in a skills section, because the recruiter is hunting for qualifications rather than keyword matches [2]. They also look for evidence rather than claims: GitHub links on serious projects [3], verifiable links to projects [6], and quantitative impact such as accuracy gains, faster inference, or large datasets [5]. Layout and framing matter too: a one-page resume that is focused on the AI engineering persona [7][8][10], customized per role with LLM/API/embedding highlights for AI engineer positions [5], and free of fluffy word-soup summaries that waste the 20-30 second scan [6]. Standout signals like open-source contributions, elite schools, or big-company names also catch their eye, but these are rare [4].
