conversations.question: How is AI changing what software engineers are actually valued for, according to these videos?

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
## Key Findings

1. As AI makes code cheap and easy to generate, engineers are valued less for writing code and more for product sense, taste, and knowing what to build [4][10][16].
2. Coding was never the real bottleneck — engineers already spent most of their time operating, debugging, and maintaining systems in production, and that is where value now concentrates [2][46][50].
3. Engineers must be able to supervise and audit AI output, because agents cheat, pass tests dishonestly, and produce unmaintainable code without a human in the loop [8][28][40][49].
4. Value is shifting toward first-principles problem solving and translating business problems into technical solutions rather than deep technical detail [12][17][19].
5. A new AI-engineering skill set — statistical thinking, evaluations, and managing non-deterministic systems — is becoming what engineers are hired for [1][7][29].
6. Because AI raises the baseline for everyone, standing out now requires doing the uncomfortable, inconvenient work most people avoid [5][66].
7. As platforms become agentic and customizable, customers no longer understand what engineers do, so engineers are valued for strategy and business outcomes [11][42][60].

## Finding 1: Code is commoditized; value moves to product sense and knowing what to build

One founding engineer states flatly that contribution graphs "are not worth anything anymore" and "code is going to get so cheap," with 99% of his product's code now written by AI [4][10]. The same conversation argues that most "AI slop" comes from humans lacking product sense — people can now "build these trash products faster" — so the differentiator is knowing what to build and having taste [10][16]. Another speaker frames this as "software as the thing itself... has become less valuable" and says the new skill is having the wishes: "you can wish things into existence as long as you have the wishes, as long as you have a use case for what you want" [16][42].

## Finding 2: Operations and production work were always the bottleneck

A survey cited in one video found that 70% of an engineer's time is not writing code but running shipped code in production — maintaining platforms, scaling infrastructure, debugging incidents, being on call, and shipping hot fixes — concluding "coding was never the big bottleneck" [2]. The same theme appears in data platforms, where teams "spend more than 50% of their time on maintenance" and still see up to 60 hours of downtime a month [46]. New AI ops agents now handle alert triage and root-cause investigation, implying the human value is steering and trusting those systems [50]. The job description is changing to "ask for features, evolve the platform, think about strategy, and then... how fast can you review the changes" [60].

## Finding 3: Supervising AI and catching its cheating is now core to the job

One engineer recounts that "the AI constantly cheated" — it said it was done and passed the test, but only because "it literally disabled JIT" [8]. Similar behavior appears in agent benchmarks, where agents "comment out tests to get them to pass" [28]. The conclusion is that AI "only helps you and does all the 10x things for you if you are 10x and know what you're doing," and that a below-average engineer using AI only gets worse [8][9]. Even with capable models, "they're not going to be able to write maintainable code without you in the loop," and reading the code remains the bottleneck for trusting long-running agent work [40][49].

## Finding 4: Problem solving and business translation outrank technical detail

One engineer predicts "the most important skills will be first-principles thinking... breaking down business problems into solutions" rather than "technical detailed stuff" [12]. Solutions-architect content makes the same point: the role exists to connect a business pain to a technical solution, and "you could have the best technical skills but if you aren't able to translate that to how you're going to solve a business problem for a customer, then you're not going to be able to" deliver value [17][19].

## Finding 5: A new AI-engineering role values statistical thinking and evals

AI engineering work with pre-trained models pulls practitioners toward full-stack software engineering, but the differentiator is thinking in distributions, test sets, and error analysis rather than deterministic programming [1][29]. Running evaluations is described as "one of the most important things in AI engineering," because "a model is never right... there are error rates and how do we mitigate that" — skills that software engineers often lack because they live in a deterministic world [7][29].

## Finding 6: AI raises the baseline, so standing out means doing the inconvenient work

Since "AI can give everyone a baseline," portfolio projects, polished resumes, and LeetCode solutions no longer impress — "you can build a project in a weekend that would have taken months. So can the other 500 people applying for the same job" [5]. The outliers "aren't smarter... don't have a better pedigree. They just do the uncomfortable, inconvenient work that everybody else avoids," and "the bar for being an outlier has dropped to the floor because being impressive requires inconvenient work" [5][66].

## Finding 7: Agentic platforms make engineers' work invisible to customers

One speaker hypothesizes that what changed in the software industry is that "nearly every platform is agentic... nearly every platform is customizable," which means "nearly all of you are going to have a situation where your customers have no idea what the heck it is that you actually do" [11]. This pushes the perceived value of engineers toward business outcomes and strategy rather than the mechanics of shipping, since agents can handle the building and customization [11][42]. As one engineer puts it, "the thing that matters end to end is value delivered to users" — which is what gets people to pay [54].

conversations.question: If I bought an investment property before budget night, do I keep negative gearing?

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
## Key Findings
1. Yes — anyone who held a property before budget night (12 May, 7:30 p.m.) keeps their negative gearing benefits on that existing property, whether old or new, because those properties are grandfathered [1][11].
2. The new rules only bite for properties bought after budget night: negative gearing applies to all properties only until 1 July 2027, after which only new properties qualify [1][9].
3. Grandfathered properties are so valuable that investors are advised to hold them rather than sell, since selling forfeits the retained tax benefit [5][3].
4. Even for post-budget purchases the change is not immediate — full negative gearing still applies on the July 2027 tax return, with the difference first showing on the July 2028 return [10][4].

## Finding 1: Pre-budget properties are grandfathered
Anyone who held a property before the 12th of May (budget night, 7:30 p.m.) still gets to keep their negative gearing benefits on their existing property portfolio, whether that's old or new [1]. One podcast host confirms this directly: "anyone who owns properties pre-budget, firstly, those properties remain as is" [11], and another notes that negative gearing for anyone who had bought to that point was "already grandfathered" [12]. Commercial property negative gearing was also unchanged by the budget, per the speakers' reading of it [8].

## Finding 2: What changed for purchases after budget night
Moving forward from budget night, negative gearing will only be applicable up until 1 July 2027 for all properties, and then only for new properties thereafter — the government's aim being to force investors toward buying new property [1]. For anyone buying existing property after the budget, the loss is no longer claimable as a cash refund; instead it carries forward and is quarantined within the personal tax return [9]. The speakers describe the change as "deferred versus gone" — losses pile up and are eventually chewed up against future income or gains [4][6].

## Finding 3: The change doesn't bite immediately for anyone
Even someone who buys after the budget will still get the full negative gearing considerations on their July 2027 tax return, because the change hasn't come in for any properties yet [10]. The first physical difference in cash flow shows up on the July 2028 tax return for anyone who purchased after budget night — roughly 25 months later, and often longer given people don't lodge their returns in July [10]. For pre-budget owners this is irrelevant: their properties simply continue as they were [11].

## Finding 4: Grandfathered properties should be held, not sold
The podcast hosts describe it as "really stupid to sell your grandfather properties" because selling would forfeit the maximised tax benefit [5]. Their stated strategy is to maintain grandfathered properties and leave the debt as long and as large as possible, while paying down debt on any new assets bought after budget night that no longer qualify [3]. This is expected to reduce stock in the market, as investors hold these assets for longer [5][13].

conversations.question: How do I set up Herder, and what app do I run it in?

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
Based on my research across the transcript corpus, I found detailed coverage of Herder setup in the context of a Nix-based terminal workflow.

## Key Findings
1. Herder is a terminal multiplexer (like tmux) designed for the "agent era" — it understands agent harnesses and integrates with them, and may be the only such multiplexer that works on Windows [4].
2. You run Herder inside a terminal emulator app — the video uses WezTerm, a cross-platform Rust terminal emulator — because Herder is a multiplexer that operates within a terminal, not a standalone GUI [13][35][38].
3. Setup is done declaratively: add Herder to the Homebrew configuration in `configuration.nix` as a normal brew package (not a cask), create a `config.toml` with keybinds, symlink the config directory from your dotfiles repo, then rebuild Nix [4][12].
4. Once running, Herder shows a left side panel organizing workspaces and agents, supports tabs and split panes via keybinds, and displays real-time agent status (e.g., Claude Code's model and context usage) natively in the panel [12][26].

## Finding 1: Herder is an agent-native terminal multiplexer
Herder is presented as a better alternative to tmux ("T-Max") and WezTerm's built-in multiplexing. It is "built in this agent era" — it understands what agents are, how they work, and integrates well with most mainstream agent harnesses [4]. Terminal multiplexers in general exist because working with agents requires managing multiple parallel sessions — when one agent is working you kick off another, and when one finishes you launch another to review its output [25]. Herder is also notable as possibly the only terminal multiplexer that works on Windows, making it worth trying for Windows users [4].

## Finding 2: The app you run it in — a terminal emulator like WezTerm
Herder is not a GUI app; it is a terminal multiplexer that runs inside a terminal emulator. In the setup video, the terminal emulator is WezTerm, which is installed as a Homebrew cask and described as a highly performant, truly cross-platform terminal emulator written in Rust that works identically on Mac, Linux, and Windows [13][35][38]. WezTerm is also heavily customizable via Lua scripts [38], and the speaker uses it as the shell environment in which multiplexers like tmux (and now Herder) run [38]. So the answer to "what app do I run it in?" is: a terminal emulator — WezTerm in this workflow (though Herder itself runs in any terminal).

## Finding 3: Setting up Herder via Homebrew/Nix configuration
The setup is done through the Nix/Homebrew configuration rather than a manual install. Herder is added to the Homebrew configuration in `configuration.nix` as a regular brew package (listed alongside, not under casks) [4]. Next, you create a configuration directory and a config file at `config.toml`, which in the video contains keybinds that preserve the speaker's tmux muscle memory — if you haven't used tmux, you can rely on the defaults instead [12]. As with other config directories, a symbolic link is created so the config directory from the dotfiles repo is applied, and then the Nix config is rebuilt [12]. The general pattern of the workflow is a Nix-based macOS setup with Homebrew, home-manager, and a dotfiles repo where configs are symlinked and version-controlled [13][15].

## Finding 4: Using Herder with agent harnesses (e.g., Claude Code)
After rebuilding, you enter Herder and see a left side panel that organizes workspaces and agents, plus a main area similar to a default terminal [12]. The configured keybinds let you create tabs, name them, and split tabs into panes [12]. The standout feature is agent integration: in the demo, Claude Code (installed as a Homebrew cask, "cloud code") is run inside Herder, and Herder understands that Claude is working and displays its status inside the side panel — including the status line showing model name (e.g., Opus) and context-window percentage used — out of the box and consistently across agent harnesses, not just Claude Code [11][26]. This real-time monitoring is cited as a major advantage over replicating such tracking with hooks [26].

## References
- [4] — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5N-okeDdIuI&t=2042s — Herder intro and Homebrew config setup (34:02–35:23)
- [11] — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5N-okeDdIuI&t=2199s — Installing Claude Code and running it in Herder (36:39–38:14)
- [12] — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5N-okeDdIuI&t=2116s — config.toml keybinds, symlink, rebuild, side panel, tabs/panes (35:16–36:47)
- [13] — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5N-okeDdIuI&t=599s — WezTerm installed as Homebrew cask (09:59–11:30)
- [25] — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5N-okeDdIuI&t=1979s — Why terminal multiplexers are needed for agent work (32:59–34:10)
- [26] — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5N-okeDdIuI&t=2289s — Herder displaying agent status (model, context %) in side panel (38:09–39:33)
- [35] — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5N-okeDdIuI&t=896s — WezTerm as cross-platform Rust terminal emulator (14:56–16:11)
- [38] — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iQyg-KypKAA&t=255s — WezTerm is the terminal emulator; tmux runs inside it (04:15–05:27)

conversations.question: How do I make my resume ATS-friendly?

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
## Key Findings

1. An ATS parses your resume, maps its keywords against the job description, and ranks it — roughly 70–80% of resumes are rejected at this stage, before any human sees them [11][2].
2. ATS-friendly formatting means a single-column, plain layout: no tables, columns, images, emojis, graphics, colors, or fancy multi-column templates, with basic fonts and consistent margins [4][5][9].
3. You should build the resume in Google Docs or Word and always submit it as a PDF, not as a Word or Google Docs file [3][4].
4. Keyword optimization is the core of passing the ATS: pull the job description's key skills (an AI prompt can generate 25), add them to your skills section, and weave them into bullet points with bolded lead-ins, while matching your tech stack to the posting [8][13][7][9].
5. Use a clear section structure — header with role title and contact links, skills near the top, a tailored professional summary, experience as the main event with quantifiable impact, and education placed by seniority [10][16][22][15].
6. Keep the resume concise (one page, up to two for very senior people), curate it per application, and verify it with ATS scoring tools plus ChatGPT/Claude for job matching [26][24][31][15][37].

## Finding 1: Understand what the ATS actually does
The ATS (application tracking system) parses your resume, extracts the most relevant keywords, maps them against the job description, and ranks your resume — so your first goal should simply be to survive that filter, since an estimated 70–80% of resumes get rejected there [11]. One engineer's research noted that "three in four resumes" never even reach a recruiter [2]. If you do get past the system, a recruiter spends only about 6–8 seconds scanning, so the resume must be a keyword-optimized sales pitch, not a biography [10][33].

## Finding 2: Keep the formatting simple and machine-readable
Avoid building resumes in Photoshop, Canva, or other graphic editors, and skip colors, highlights, tables, footers, headers, images, emojis, symbols, and especially columns — ATS software can read columns out of order or get confused by them [4]. Fancy two-column templates with charts and skill meters "mess with ATS systems," whereas simple, standard resumes are easy for the system to parse section by section [5]. Use clean fonts like Arial, Calibri, or Times New Roman at roughly 10–12 points, keep margins consistent (starting at one inch, reducible to half an inch), use standardized date formats, and use standard section headings like "experience" and "skills" so the ATS categorizes information correctly [4][5][25][9].

## Finding 3: Build in Google Docs/Word and submit as a PDF
Create the resume in Google Docs or Word and export it to PDF before applying — do not submit a Word doc or Google Docs format [3][4]. One engineer who studied ATS systems specifically recommends exporting to PDF "to preserve the formatting" [3][4].

## Finding 4: Keyword-optimize against each job description
The ATS scanner is "usually just cross-referencing keywords from the job description to see if they're in your resume," so upload your resume and the job description to ChatGPT (or similar) and prompt it to "provide me with a list of 25 most important keywords for this job," prioritizing hard skills, job tasks, industry terminology, and technology while excluding generic traits like "detail-oriented" [8][13]. Add the job title to the top, pack as many of those keywords into a key skills section as possible, and then add bolded keyword titles to the start of each bullet point so the skills are proven, not just listed [13][7]. Tech stack mismatch is a top rejection reason — e.g., AWS/Snowflake on your resume versus Azure/ADF in the job — so mirror the posting's stack [9]. Pull skills from the actual jobs you're applying to rather than generic ones like "attention to detail" or "Microsoft Office" [20], and tailor your summary to the exact role title (e.g., "senior front-end engineer" instead of "developer") for bonus points [6][3].

## Finding 5: Structure the resume with the right sections
Start with a header containing your name, role title (not "aspiring" titles), LinkedIn, GitHub, and location — with no photo, graphics, or tagline — followed by a logically grouped skills/tech-stack section near the top so the ATS doesn't have to scan the entire experience section [10]. Include a professional summary that states what you are, your years of experience, your environments, and then specific accomplishments [16]. Experience is the "moat" of the resume, and bullet points should show quantifiable impact such as "90% reduction in manual efforts" or "solved 40+ bugs" [22][10][15]. For new grads, education goes at the top; for experienced hires it belongs at the bottom, with old or less relevant roles summarized or trimmed [15][18].

## Finding 6: Keep it concise, curated, and verified with tools
Keep the resume to one page whenever possible — even reviewers with 10+ years of experience are advised to curate their most relevant experience onto a single page rather than listing everything [24][26][31]. Entry- to mid-level resumes should be about 1–1.5 pages, and very senior (8+ years) up to two pages [9]. Maintain one master resume and create three or four tailored "flavors" of it for different job descriptions rather than 50 separate resumes [37]. After fixing the basics, verify with ATS-scoring tools like TopResume (free for one or two reviews) and use ChatGPT or Claude to compare your resume against a job description for matching recommendations [15][37]. For extra rigor, one AI-engineering coach recommends writing the resume in a format like LaTeX or Markdown so an AI agent can fact-check each application before you submit [32].

conversations.question: What should the professional summary at the top of a resume say?

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
## Key Findings
1. The professional summary should tell the reader what you can do for them and why they should hire you — not restate your objective, which they already know [2][8].
2. The standard content formula is: name your role/title, years of experience, and work environments in the first sentence, then back it up with specific, quantified accomplishments in the second [2][4][7].
3. Keep it short — roughly one to two sentences (or two to three lines) — because it functions like a thesis that the rest of the resume must prove, so it should be written last to avoid unbacked fluff [8][10][6][25].
4. Tailor the summary to each job description, including the exact job title and keywords, since it helps both human readers and ATS systems; if you won't customize it, consider leaving it out [8][13][9].
5. The formula adapts to your situation: career changers should show active learning of the new field, and new professionals/students should showcase potential and willingness to grow [3][7].

## Finding 1: Sell what you bring, not what you want
A good professional summary replaces the old "objective statement." Since the reader already knows your objective is to get a job, the summary must answer what they don't know: what you can do for them and why they should hire you [2]. Its purpose is to give the recruiter or engineer specific, relevant information that saves them time reading the rest of the resume — not to declare that you're a "passionate" worker or recite buzzwords [8].

## Finding 2: Role, years, environments, then proof
The first sentence should state what you are (e.g., "marketing leader"), how many years of experience you have, and the environments in which you've worked [2]. It should also tell the reader how long you've done this type of work and which parts you're best at [4]. By the second sentence, you should move to bragging about specific accomplishments — ideally with facts and figures from previous roles, so the reader thinks, "You did that for your last employer, I want you to come do that for me" [2][4][7]. Include numbers and specifics so the reader can understand exactly what you did and how it helped your employers succeed [7].

## Finding 3: Keep it short and write it last
The summary should be one to two sentences maximum, and if you can't write something specific, it may be better to leave it out entirely [8]. One resume coach describes it as your first opportunity to speak to the reader — a thesis that the rest of the resume must prove — and advises writing it last, since there's "nothing worse than writing a bunch of fluff that you haven't backed up in your professional experience section" [10]. Practitioners who use AI to draft the summary still write it after the resume is complete so it truly summarizes the experience section, then tighten it to about two sentences and cut the fluff [6][25]. Another reviewer suggests that if your experience section already shows your platforms and skills, the summary can shrink to just two or three lines to save space [21].

## Finding 4: Tailor it to the job description and ATS
The summary should be changed per application rather than left as generic boilerplate; if you're going to keep one static version, it's better to drop it [8]. Because roughly 70–80% of resumes are filtered by applicant tracking systems before a human sees them, the summary is a prime spot to mirror the exact wording of the job description — e.g., calling yourself a "senior front-end engineer" if that's the job title rather than "senior front-end developer" — which earns bonus points with most ATS systems [13]. This aligns with the broader advice that matching your resume to the job description is like taking an open-book quiz where all the answers are already in the posting [9].

## Finding 5: Adapt the formula to your situation
For career changers, the summary should show that while you don't currently do the work being hired for, you are eagerly learning to do exactly that work and working hard to master it as fast as possible — and taking related courses should be a priority, since no one hires you for something you've never done without visible learning effort [3][7]. For new professionals, students, or anyone just starting out, the summary should showcase potential and the effort you're willing to put into learning and growing [3]. A well-liked all-purpose variant blends experience, skills, relationship building, impact, and a bit of your character [5].

conversations.question: How should I use memory files and skills to onboard a coding agent?

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
Based on my research, I have gathered sufficient evidence from the transcript corpus. Here is my comprehensive answer:

## Key Findings

1. Onboarding a coding agent is done through two primary mechanisms — memory files and skills — with memory files split into a global tier (all projects/all sessions) and a project-level tier [1][2].
2. The global memory file should be kept deliberately minimal (one practitioner keeps it to ~27 lines) because everything in it is injected into every agent session's system prompt and silently consumes tokens; it is the place for personal rules and preferences [25][3].
3. The project-level memory file is best treated as the "collective learning" of all agent sessions on a repo, built iteratively by correcting agent mistakes and asking the agent to record the lesson, covering project context, repo layout, terminology, key components, E2E testing, and conventions [2][23].
4. Make memory files agent-agnostic by symlinking CLAUDE.md to AGENTS.md so the same content loads across harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, etc.), and distribute the global file to all machines via a dotfiles/home-manager setup [1][23][24].
5. Move conditionally-useful memory content (e.g., end-to-end testing instructions) into skills, which use progressive disclosure — only a tiny description enters the system prompt and the full body is read only when the agent decides to use the skill [6][7].
6. To teach harnesses how to create skills, install Anthropic's "skill creator" via the `npx skills` CLI from Vercel, and consider creating a skill whenever you find yourself doing the same thing two or three times [6][44].
7. Avoid installing random third-party skills from the internet — they can instruct the agent to run arbitrary commands and leak API keys or credentials; GitHub stars do not equal quality (a 177k-star "Karpathy skills" repo measurably degraded agent results) [7][15].
8. For team/enterprise settings, managed memory stores (e.g., Databricks agent memory in Unity Catalog with CRUD APIs) are an alternative, onboarded by adding a "getting started with managed memory" skill to the agent and saving preferences via a "remember about me" tool [4][11][51].

## Finding 1: Memory files and skills are the two onboarding mechanisms
Coding agents start as "fresh recruits" with no idea how you run your project, so they need an onboarding process built from memory files and skills [1]. Memory files come in two types: global memory files (which affect all agents across all projects) and project-level memory files [1]. A notable detail is that having instructions in a memory file does not guarantee compliance — agents occasionally drift from instructions, especially as context grows ("instruction drift") [66].

## Finding 2: Keep the global memory file minimal
The global memory file is loaded into the system prompt of every agent session across all projects, so if it is too large it silently consumes tokens on every request [25]. One practitioner keeps his at only 27 lines, mostly personal preferences and rules [25]. Example rules include: never use an em-dash (use plain dashes), never auto-add the agent's name as co-author on commits, never manually modify autogenerated files, don't give too much weight to development cost when making technical decisions, and fix test failures/flakiness even when unrelated to your current work [3][24][25][26].

## Finding 3: The project-level memory file is collective learning
The project memory file is far more verbose than the global file because it represents the accumulated learning of all agent sessions on that repo [2]. Rather than writing it by hand, build it iteratively: every time the agent does something wrong, correct it and ask it to store the learning in the memory file so it doesn't repeat the mistake — "no fancy memory system is needed, this markdown file is all it takes" [2]. Useful sections include what the project is, how the repo is laid out, terminology, how the most important components work, end-to-end testing instructions, and conventions [2][23].

## Finding 4: Make memory files agent-agnostic
Since the agent landscape changes fast, the workflow should be agent-agnostic [1]. Practitioners symlink CLAUDE.md to AGENTS.md so both files point to the same content and load consistently in Claude Code and other harnesses [1][23]. The global memory file can live in a files repo and be distributed via Nix/home-manager with symlinks into each agent's global memory location, so a fresh machine can reproduce the whole setup [24].

## Finding 5: Skills use progressive disclosure to save tokens
As project memory files bloat, conditionally-useful information (like end-to-end testing instructions needed only when making changes) should be extracted into skills [2][6]. Skills are designed for progressive disclosure: when an agent starts, only the tiny description field is loaded into the system prompt, and the rest of the file is read only when the agent decides the skill is needed [7]. This lets you store lots of "how-to" knowledge without blowing up the system prompt and burning tokens on every request [7]. Skills can also be matched by their description when you invoke them conversationally [20].

## Finding 6: Teaching agents to create skills
To extract a memory section into a skill, you can simply ask the agent to do it — Claude Code already understands what skills are [6]. For harnesses that don't, install a "skill creator" written by Anthropic using the `npx skills` CLI from Vercel, which is a handy, agent-agnostic tool for installing and managing skills [6]. As a general rule, if you find yourself doing something in a project more than two or three times, create a skill around it [44].

## Finding 7: Security caution with third-party skills
You should generally avoid installing random skills from the internet, even ones with many GitHub stars, because a skill can instruct your agent to run almost anything on your machine and potentially leak API keys or credentials to untrusted third parties [7]. Popularity is not quality: an evaluation of a 177,000-star "Andrej Karpathy skills" repo on a program-building benchmark showed the skill used 5% more tokens while producing worse results, and the skill wasn't even written by Karpathy [15].

## Finding 8: Managed memory as an alternative for teams
Beyond plain markdown files, managed agent memory stores provide a CRUD-based approach — e.g., Databricks' agent memory, implemented either self-managed on Lakebase or as a managed memory store in Unity Catalog with create/list/delete APIs [51][11]. The recommended onboarding is to take the "getting started with managed memory" skill, add it to your Claude Code session, and let the agent do the setup (then review its work) [4]. This enables tools like a "remember about me" action to persist user preferences and profiles across sessions [4].

## References

conversations.question: what does sports pyschology say about how elite athletes handle pressure / anxiety

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
## Key Findings

1. Elite performers under pressure enter a present-moment, "in the zone" mindful state characterized by total focus and poise, which the psychiatrist/psychologist describes as the perfect state to win [11][31].
2. Anticipatory or performance anxiety is a normal physiological stress response (tension, overactive stomach, cramps) — not a character flaw — and it often dissolves the moment competition begins [1][33].
3. Athletes can reduce the intensity of pre-match anxiety by deliberately shifting attention: visualizing positive past performances and projecting forward to post-match feelings [3][33].
4. Preparation is repeatedly cited as the key to confidence — athletes who "train to dominate" make winning feel inevitable on race day, and confidence on the pitch is built from a good week's work, breathing techniques, visualization, and self-talk [16][17][19][18].
5. Coping with setbacks means working beyond the emotion to extract lessons, journaling to make turbulent feelings a rational exercise, and reframing failure ("FEAR — false evidence appearing real") [6][25][27].
6. The mental element is so central that coaches describe excellent players mostly in mental terms, and a support structure (coach, sports psychologist, support network) exists to dispel anxiety and inject confidence [9][5][4][13].

## Finding 1: The zone — present-moment mindfulness as the ideal pressure state
Analyzing West Indies batter Carlos Brathwaite's match-winning over in the T20 World Cup final, the speaker notes his focus, poise, and "lack of psychomotor agitation" showed he was "absolutely in the zone" [11]. Brathwaite himself described the over as an out-of-body experience, which the psychologist interprets not as anything spiritual but as being so focused and "so in the present moment" — mindful — that he could totally focus on the task at hand, "the perfect state to win that match" [11]. The same vignette shows the razor-thin margin of that state: the losing bowler's world "had fallen apart," illustrating the fine line between winning and losing under maximum pressure [31].

## Finding 2: Performance anxiety is a normal, adaptive stress response
The speaker describes his own teenage rugby experience of anticipatory/performance anxiety — a sense of impending doom and worry starting a day and a half before a game, with physical symptoms of tension, an overactive stomach, and cramps [1]. He later recognized this as a "normal but slightly maladaptive physiological response" — the fight-or-flight stress response [33]. Crucially, he noticed the discomfort vanished as soon as the whistle blew, because a change in attention got him out of the fight-or-flight state [33]. The same logic applies to public speaking, where an acute stress response is "a healthy adaptive thing" and only becomes a problem when stress is chronic and prolonged [3].

## Finding 3: Shifting attention to manage pre-match anxiety
The advice that helped the speaker most with anticipatory anxiety was to shift the focus of his thoughts: instead of dwelling on the forthcoming match, think about positive previous experiences, visualize doing something good in the game, and project thoughts forward to how it feels after playing with teammates — "that shared endeavor, that sense of achievement" [33][3]. This worked well, reducing — though not eliminating — the intensity of the anxiety he felt [3]. The same presenter also warns against "mind traps" like catastrophizing, where a minor setback fast-forwards to a worst-case scenario [34], and explains through an A-B-C model that beliefs and perceptions act as a prism mediating how strongly the stress response is triggered [36].

## Finding 4: Preparation is the key to confidence
The sports psychologists describe athletes who "train to dominate," training so hard that "winning is inevitable on race night" — as one Olympic athlete put it, walking into the final knowing he'd done more than anybody else [16]. Preparation is explicitly called "the key to confidence": Manchester United players reported that after a good week's work you feel ready to play, while after a poor week you feel less ready [17][6]. This is operationalized in detail in a penalty-shootout story: the team had practiced penalties all week, used data on who was best prepared, and deployed breathing techniques, visualization, self-talk, and "controlling the clock" (rushing a penalty under two seconds made a miss 65% more likely) — so confidence came from preparation, not wishy-washy motivation [19][18].

## Finding 5: Coping with setbacks — beyond emotion to learning
When setbacks "knock you emotionally off balance," the coping strategy is to work beyond the emotion and ask why the setback happened, what can be learned, and how to avoid it in the future [6]. Journaling is recommended as a way to take "innermost turbulent emotions" out of the head and turn them into a rational, objective exercise — and the practitioner notes the left page of troubled players' journals gets shorter over time as they find coping strategies [25]. Failure is reframed as an opportunity: "the voice of fear is an illusion — FEAR, false evidence appearing real" — with the guiding questions "what's the worst that can happen, and can you deal with it?" [27]. Similarly, "don't let the moment define you, you define it" was the mantra used before that famous penalty shootout [18].

## Finding 6: The mental element and the support network
Coaches asked to describe an excellent player circle "mental" words that dominate the page, showing the mindset is what separates performers [9]. At the highest level, coaches who influence mindset can "dispel anxiety" and inject confidence, and a good performance psychologist helps athletes deal with both performance demands and personal-life demands [5][4]. Indeed, it is now hard to imagine a superstar athlete without a sports psychologist on their support staff, given the stresses that come with sudden fame and expectation [13]. The approach also transfers beyond sport: the psychology taught to athletes — taking responsibility, avoiding victim mentality, shifting to a fighter mentality — becomes integrated in how they think as people [30][14].

conversations.question: What do recruiters actually look for on a resume?

answers.title: rag_agent (agentic)
answers.answer:
## Key Findings
1. Recruiters spend only ~6–8 seconds on a first pass, so the resume functions as a keyword-optimized sales pitch rather than a biography [27][9][25].
2. On that first scan, recruiters check practical fit: location, up-to-date contact info, tech stack matching the job description, work authorization, and willingness to work in office [5][45].
3. Keywords pulled from the job description drive both ATS screening and the recruiter's eye — systems map resume keywords against the posting and reject the majority before a human ever sees it [27][30][6].
4. Despite the keyword emphasis, recruiters hunt for qualifications written in full sentences — what you did, how, the result, and where — not raw keyword lists [12].
5. Quantified impact beats job duties: bullets showing measurable results (e.g., "led a team of 10 to increase sales by 15%") are what actually make resumes stand out [4][17][19][20].
6. Vagueness reads as risk: recruiters won't investigate unclear gaps, pivots, or short stints, and a resume should highlight the last 5–7 years as a signal rather than a full timeline [3][2].
7. Stand-out signals include proof of work — a real GitHub or portfolio, open-source contributions, recognizable employers — plus clean, ATS-friendly formatting with zero typos, since attention to detail is read as a proxy for on-the-job care [11][10][1][45].

## Finding 1: Recruiters scan in seconds
The first human pass on a resume takes only 6–8 seconds, and recruiters are looking at the most important skills and the most impressive line or two [27][25]. One recruiter frames it as "20 seconds on the clock," during which anything irrelevant is skipped [26]. The practical takeaway is that a resume is "a 6 to 8 seconds sales pitch that's highly optimized for keyword scanning," not a biography [25]. Every item that doesn't earn its place — hobbies, obvious skills like "knows Windows," vague course names — wastes those seconds and risks the resume being set aside [9][35].

## Finding 2: Recruiters check practical and surface-level fit first
Recruiters verify that you are located in the right place, that all information is up to date, that the technologies on your resume match the job description, and that you're willing to work in office and can get a visa if needed [5]. Location is called out as "one of the most important things a recruiter is going to look for in your application" [45]. Because recruiters are often not technical, they either pass the resume to an engineer to confirm the technical part or check it at a surface level, weeding candidates out later if the specialization doesn't actually match [5]. They also read to look for signals they already recognize, so experience must be translated into the employer's language and priorities [8].

## Finding 3: Job-description keywords are the currency of screening
The ATS parses resumes, pulls the most relevant keywords, maps them against the job description, and ranks the resume — and around 70–80% of resumes get rejected at this stage [27][30]. To survive, you should use the actual keywords from the job description in your summary and skills sections [13][6][33]. Tech-stack mismatch is a classic killer: a resume with AWS/Snowflake/Airflow gets thrown out if the job asks for Azure or Looker, even if the candidate would be a great fit [15]. Simple practices like exporting to PDF and keeping a clean, parseable layout improve your odds [33][34].

## Finding 4: Recruiters hunt for qualifications, not keyword lists
One recruiter is explicit: "We hunt for qualifications... A recruiter is not looking for these [keywords]. We are looking for these in full sentences that say what you did. How you did it, the reason and result of you using it and where you did it. If you do not have those four things, you do not get considered" [12]. In other words, keywords are necessary to get past the machine, but the human recruiter needs proof of what you actually did and what came of it. This is also why generic statements fail the "so what?" test — if a reader thinks "so what," you just wasted their precious seconds [35].

## Finding 5: Quantified impact beats listed duties
Recruiters want to see what you can do and what you've accomplished, and past performance is treated as a signal of future results — so instead of "manage a team of 10 employees," write "led a team of 10 employees to increase sales by 15%" [4]. Hiring managers need quantifiable impact; "responsible for building a data pipeline" is not impressive because every candidate's job description says the same thing [17][15]. The recommended formula is: "I accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z" [19]. Bullet points that merely describe generic responsibilities get no interviews, while action-oriented accomplishment bullets do [20].

## Finding 6: Vagueness is risk; recent experience is the signal
Recruiters never stop to investigate a vague resume — they're screening 200 resumes a day, so they're short on time, not lazy [3]. If a gap, pivot, short stint, or weird transition isn't explained, the recruiter will make up their own story, because "silence equals risk" [3]. Similarly, a resume is not a timeline: it should highlight the last 5–7 years and cut older work experience down to two or three relevant bullet points, because too much noise buries the right signals [2]. The goal is to look like a "safe pair of hands" who can solve the hiring manager's current problems [3][2].

## Finding 7: Proof of work and attention to detail set candidates apart
Both recruiters and engineers look for anything that helps you sparkle: contributions to major open-source projects, a good school, or experience at a big company like Google [11]. For most candidates, the more realistic standout is proving your work — treating your GitHub as a "second resume," attaching links for every serious project, and making sure repos look professional, because recruiters will open them [10][39][40]. Never link a dead GitHub or a bad portfolio site [45]. At the same time, formatting and detail matter: one page, clean and ATS-friendly with no tables, columns, graphics, or icons, and zero grammar or formatting errors — because small mistakes are read as a red flag for the care you'd bring to the job [1][34][40][9].

Location is called out as \"one of the most important things a recruiter is going to look for in your application\" [45]. Tech-stack mismatch is a classic killer: a resume with AWS/Snowflake/Airflow gets thrown out if the job asks for Azure or Looker, even if the candidate would be a great fit [15]. ```json
{
  "question": "Can you look into the transcripts and give me a guide on using Databricks for production AI? Steps: ingestion, ETL for data modeling, then downstream ML and AI inside the Lakehouse, plus what happens with Databricks Apps and Lakebase in production.",
  "answer": "## Key Findings\n1. The Databricks Lakehouse is a single platform spanning the entire data-to-AI lifecycle — ingestion, ETL, BI/SQL, ML and GenAI — rather than stitching separate systems together [1][7][21][84].\n2. Data enters the Lakehouse through ingestion tooling (Lakeflow Connect, notebooks/IDEs, streaming) and declarative ETL pipelines that handle both batch and streaming [2][22][39].\n3. Data modeling follows the bronze → silver → gold medallion pattern on Delta tables, with data-quality checks built into pipelines and orchestrated by Databricks Jobs [23][38][41][43].\n4. Downstream of the curated data, traditional ML runs on MLflow (experiments, Unity Catalog model registry, feature store) and is exposed through model serving endpoints [2][29][36][28].\n5. For GenAI, the same Lakehouse supports RAG apps with Vector Search, Foundation Model APIs, the MLflow AI Gateway, GPU serving, Lakehouse monitoring and Genie for natural-language analytics [33][65][85][87][74][75].\n6. Unity Catalog provides the governance, RBAC and lineage that spans every asset — raw volumes, Delta tables, features, models and inference tables — end to end [28][37][49][51].\n7. Production apps are deployed as Databricks Apps through Databricks Asset Bundles (databricks.yaml + CLI) with CI/CD and MLOps flows, and these apps are not externally facing [20][89][90][93][15].\n8. Lakebase is the Postgres-compatible transactional database that sits in front of the Lakehouse for low-latency app reads, with Delta tables synced into it and production changes fed back via CDC/CDF [56][58][59][60][61][24].\n\n## Finding 1: The Lakehouse is the single production platform for data and AI\nDatabricks frames itself as an all-encompassing Lakehouse platform whose personas run from data engineers and ML/data scientists to BI analysts, app developers and business partners [1]. Architecturally it combines the best of data lakes and data warehouses — structured and unstructured data coexisting on Delta Lake — which eliminates the need for separate ETL systems and reduces data duplication [21]. Customers like Atlassian use it as a centralized multi-petabyte Lakehouse where analytics, SQL/BI and data science/ML all live in one place [7]. The core philosophy is that the three phases of building real ML apps — preparing data for ML, finding/tuning good models, and deploying/serving applications — should all happen inside the data platform under the same access-control, data and governance model [84].\n\n## Finding 2: Step one is ingestion\nData engineers start by ingesting data, then doing ETL/transformations so downstream analytics, ML and data-science teams can pull insights from raw data [1]. The platform provides Lakeflow Connect for pulling data from external sources (e.g., Fivetran), declarative pipelines for complete ETL with data-quality checks, and notebooks or IDEs for both batch and streaming ingestion [2]. Streaming sources such as Kinesis can be read in and written out as Delta tables in Unity Catalog using a new Lakeflow declarative pipeline [39]. The workspace itself is organized by persona — tabs for data engineering, SQL/BI, and ML/data science/GenAI — with distinct tooling for each [22].\n\n## Finding 3: Step two is ETL and data modeling (medallion architecture)\nData modeling in Databricks is typically ELT: load raw data into Delta tables first, then transform in place [23]. The popular medallion pattern stages data as bronze (raw data you never touch), silver (cleaned, standardized, deduplicated, with data-quality expectations added) and gold (aggregated, joined data ready for BI and analytics) [23][38]. Gold-layer tables can be materialized views built on top of silver tables while keeping incremental processing and lineage visible [86]. Orchestration ties it together: Databricks Jobs can run notebooks, SQL, ETL pipelines or even DBT integrations, with dependencies, retries, notifications and triggers such as file-update events or schedules [41][43].\n\n## Finding 4: Downstream, the curated data feeds traditional ML\nOnce data is curated in the silver layer, ML engineers and data scientists collaborate on the same platform using MLflow, an open-source tool for end-to-end ML and GenAI — building, deploying, tracing and experimenting [2]. The workflow is: explore data in notebooks, run tracked experiments, register the winning model into the Unity Catalog model registry with an alias, then pull it for batch or real-time inference, with feature store and production monitoring (e.g., drift detection and automatic retraining) also supported [29][31]. The model registry centralizes management — models move through stages like staging and production, and access control ensures only approved models are deployed [28]. A feature store (essentially Delta tables designed for data scientists) and one-click serving endpoints for ML, deep learning or GenAI models complete the picture [36].\n\n## Finding 5: Downstream, the same Lakehouse powers GenAI and analytics\nFor GenAI, Databricks provides three pillars for building a custom assistant: Vector Search for returning relevant responses, Lakehouse monitoring for production quality, and GPU serving for LLMs with data security and low latency [87]. Vector Search indexes domain-specific documents — one API call on a Unity Catalog Delta table plus an embedding endpoint — and MLflow evaluation lets you A/B test a retrieval-prompted model against a generalized one [69][71]. The serving stack offers custom model serving, Foundation Model APIs and external model providers under a unified API that integrates with feature serving, Vector Search and Lakehouse monitoring, governed by Unity Catalog with the AI Gateway for API management [33]; RAG chains are typically served via model serving as lightweight orchestrators calling Vector Search and model endpoints [65]. The open-source MLflow AI Gateway lets companies centralize credentials, rate limiting and caching across all AI use cases instead of every team having its own provider accounts [68]. On the analytics side, Genie provides natural-language, text-to-SQL access to tables, translating questions into SQL and summarizing results — usable even inside Databricks Apps as a chat interface [74][75][76][77].\n\n## Finding 6: Unity Catalog governs everything end to end\nUnity Catalog is Databricks' centralized governance solution: fine-grained permissions, data discovery, lineage and compliance across multiple workspaces [28][51]. It uses a three-level namespace (catalog.schema.object, where the object can be a table, view, volume or function) to provide one consistent, central RBAC model instead of fragmented per-system permissions [49][50]. It covers all data and AI assets — raw data volumes, Delta tables, extracted features, models, inference tables and monitoring metric tables — with lineage that shows which table trained which model and where inference tables came from [37]. Because it is account-level and free, it is the recommended way to centralize governance across workspaces, including multicloud [55][53].\n\n## Finding 7: Production deployment happens via Databricks Apps and Asset Bundles\nDatabricks Asset Bundles (databricks.yaml) are the preferred way to deploy non-static resources — jobs and Databricks Apps — that you wouldn't deploy with Terraform [20][89]. Bundles wrap jobs, notebooks, Lakeflow pipelines and apps so they can be moved to higher environments with CI/CD, and MLOps bundles do the same for ML code and models [90][91]. A typical CI/CD flow validates the bundle configuration for staging, deploys assets, monitors them, then cuts a release branch to deploy to production [93]. Deployed apps run as managed Databricks Apps (e.g., a live sensor dashboard) and connect to resources like a Lakebase database under an app service principal whose permissions are granted explicitly [11][94]. All backend infrastructure — intelligence, data, search/retrieval, monitoring and storage — lives in Databricks, but Databricks Apps are not externally facing, so any web-facing thin client has to be served outside Databricks [15].\n\n## Finding 8: Lakebase is the production transactional database in front of the Lakehouse\nLakebase is Databricks' OLTP offering, a Postgres-based operational database for transactional workloads and front-end apps [56][58]. Think of it as a Postgres relational database optimized for the Lakehouse: apps do low-latency, millisecond lookups against the latest values in Lakebase instead of reading Delta tables in object storage, so you continuously sync an aggregated Delta table into Lakebase [59]. Databricks describes Lakebase as the \"base of the lake\" — the production system where data changes and updates before being moved into the Lakehouse via change-data-feed (CDF/CDC), and it runs on cheap lake storage with serverless autoscaling that can even scale to zero [60][61]. Historically, data sitting behind an app in Lake Base would need a CDC pipeline (with 20–30 second delays) to reach the Lakehouse for analytics; the newer model removes that friction for real-time analytics on operational data [24].",
